The reason for SkARGB32_Shader_Blitter::blitMask not supporting shaders with non-src-over xfer modes with anything other than a8 is that SkXfermode::xfer32 only supports A8. The local 'blend_row' is essentially an out-of-line set of specializations for SkXfermode::xfer32 for src-over.

subject: pdf: Implement SkColorSpace on SaveLayerRec using ICC color profiles
message:
A gm means adding a "golden master" test, like the ones under the `gm/` directory in the Skia repository. These can then be viewed in the `viewer` application, are run by the `dm` application which runs tests, and run by `dm` on the waterfall (all the `Test-` tasks at status.skia.org) with the results uploaded to gold.skia.org where they can be viewed and triaged.

The icc profiles in the PDF are there for the obvious reasons and most viewers do use them, though support for anything in PDF that isn't "draw a solid fill rectangle" seems to vary across viewers. For example, Pdfium is currently in an experiment to move off of its old rendering backend onto a newer Skia rendering backend for (among other things) proper color space support.

Generally we try to ensure there is a GM for things like this so we can muck about with it in `viewer` and ensure manually that it's rendering correctly with all the Skia rendering paths and also because all GMs can be output to PDF like `dm --config pdf -w <where to put output>` and then the PDF can be viewed wherever.

subject: Reland "Migrate SkParagraph's tests etc to provide SkUnicode"
message:
The entire point of having an `SkUnicode` interface is so we wouldn't need to do things like this. The `paragraph_bindings.cpp` part is meh, but all of these changes under `modules/skparagraph` are basically "why did we even try".

The fundamental design issue as I see it is anything using `fUsingClientInfo`. I'm not sure why this exists or why it is set when only some of the setters are called. The client should be creating the SkUnicode and passing it in. The user should be making this `fClientUnicodeFactory` call themselves and passing the resulting `SkUnicode` into the existing `ParagraphBuilder::make` (and all the `ParagraphBuilderImpl::set*` that touch `fUsingClientInfo` be removed).

Now, I see why this change is attractive from the standpoint of not changing the CanvasKit Paragraph API which currently just always uses the default `SkUnicode` implementation and doesn't appear to have a way to construct a `SkUnicode_client` to pass in. However, the real fix here is to have CanvasKit provide an API to create an `SkUnicode_client` (if built with that support) and then provide a way to pass that in to the paragraph.

subject: Reland "Migrate SkParagraph's tests etc to provide SkUnicode"
message: For some reason not yet determined, this appears to be causing the `OptimizeForSize-All` jobs to fail, particularly when running `paragraph__underline_visitor`.

subject: Reland "Migrate SkParagraph's tests etc to provide SkUnicode"
message:
For example calling these functions down here is currently just a super awkward (and non-atomic) way of setting up an `SkUnicode_client`. The user should just pass in the SkUnicode they want to be used instead.

Currently the way that works is Flutter builds CanvasKit without any real built in SkUnicode implementation (just the client one) which wouldn't work except for this weird API where by calling enough of these setters Paragraph will magically create a SkUnicode_client out of them.

However, we don't always want `skparagraph` to be directly depending on `SkUnicode_client`, because no one else wants or needs that code hanging around. So the proposal here is to add yet more complexity so the user can pass through a function pointer to create an `SkUnicode_client` later *out of information the user going to pass in*. The user already has all the information to create an `SkUnicode_client` and they should just make it and pass it in.

subject: Add SkColorSpace to SaveLayerRec
message:
We would need someone to work on PDF.

Currently the model in Skia's PDF emitter is that the PDF itself is always in sRGB (the PDF viewer of course can map that into any color space it wants when rendering the PDF). Recently I managed to get the color profiles of images into the PDF. That's the extent of color profiles in PDF at the moment.

As for layers, I believe that's all handled by `SkPDFDevice::createDevice` and `SkPDFDevice::drawDevice`. We try to return a PDF backed device, but if the layer paint has an image filter or color filter on it the layer device is currently a very default bitmap device which `drawDevice` will essentially treat like any other bitmap image draw.

If it's just a matter of tagging the layers with a color space, PDF can do that, but someone would need to make that work. For testing we would probably want a gm that does what this `Canvas_saveLayer_colorSpace` test does so one can take a look at the PDF output (and also test all the other configurations, like gpu and serialization).

subject: Fix shaping in GN builds
message:
It is horrifically broken to define these here. This BUILD.gn file shouldn't know anything about when or how these are set. We might as well start `#define public private`.

I'm assuming that this `canvaskit` isn't getting these because it doesn't have a direct dependency on skshaper and skunicode. However, it did previously have a hidden dependency on them trough the global. Now that we're making this application responsible for the global it needs to know about this directly.

It looks like for the time being //modules/canvaskit:canvaskit_js is depending on //modules/skottie:skottie which is doing all the depending. This does in fact mean that //modules/skottie:skottie needs to re-export these if the application is going to handle the global (otherwise we need this very error prone manual dependency here on how Skia was built).

In the end, if one isn't using the legacy globals and depending on the new build, then what ever code is doing that needs to either re-implement those globals (though perhaps not as globals) or it needs to explicitly pass the buck up the build chain. In this case //modules/skottie:skottie is still depending on skunicode and skshaper implementations, when in this forced component build it should not be (only depending on the core parts). It is this level that should be depending on the implementations. If it isn't, then it should be using the legacy globals and build.

subject: [fontations] Modernize family name
message:
This is a quite common operation that should probably be in a library. It doesn't seem like every user of Fontations should need to know this level of minutia for the common task of just wanting a family or style name. For instance, FreeType exposes this as `family_name` and `style_name` with DirectWrite providing a more modern (and more like Fontations) IDWriteFontFamily::GetFamilyNames (family names, like this) and IDWriteFont::GetFaceNames (style names, like "Regular" or "Bold") which return a set of localized strings much like `localized_strings` but automatically pick the `StringId`.

Perhaps that what Fontations should expose, a `FontRef.family_name() -> StringId` and a `FontRef.style_name() -> StringId` which would look at the WWS and which name ids are available and return which `StringId` should be requested. (They could also return the appropriate `LocalizedStrings` directly if that makes sense.)

We still need to know here if the values were present or not (to set the flags). I'm only setting these to 0 here to ensure that they are initialized to something (so `SkFontMetrics::operator==` can work). We also need to set the flag. Now we could handle this in the ffi, setting the values to 0 if not present and also having explicit boolean flags for if the values were present or not. It's just that floats already have a NaN and we know that's not a good value for a position or thickness.

I suppose this could be clearer if this setting to 0 were in an `else`, or maybe in a complicated ternary, like this beauty with a comma operator:

```
out_metrics->fUnderlinePosition = !sk_float_isnan(metrics.underline_position)
    ? out_metrics->fFlags |= SkFontMetrics::kUnderlinePositionIsValid_Flag
    , -metrics.underline_position
    : 0;
```

message: As public API it would probably be best for this to return an SkStream instead of an SkData. Most of the users of this want it just to write it out somewhere else, so it would be best to avoid the potential of copying all the data just to flatten it if we're just going to write it back out somewhere else, or just read it. This was made SkData here because the old interface wanted to return an SkData, but that wasn't ideal either.

subject: Add SkCodec API to preserve original data
message:
I like `getData` since this isn't really a conversion (and also because of the above comment). Though I understand `asData` since these both views onto a block of data, but on the other hand the SkStream also holds an offset into that data (`toData` wouldn't be right though, there isn't any conversion).

I think it's probably ok to keep both of these, since `getMemoryBase` is lower overhead (no need to ref) to get a borrowed reference instead of a shared one. So we can just remove the "TODO" comment above.

And where is it used ([looks like just in StreamTest.cpp](https://skia.googlesource.com/skia.git/+/32f1cb50734a4a5dad0c54b4a06ad8bdce2e7be5/tests/StreamTest.cpp#194))?

subject: Add SkCodec API to preserve original data
message:
It seems really awkward to pass this back in, and seems really strange to put on Codec, especially when we already have SkImage_Lazy and SkImageGenerator which are designed to handle this. Also, we need an actual answer for users to create lazy images which seems to be somewhat lacking at the moment, though I'm not sure if they're required now?

Also, this got me thinking about why this is a SkData and not SkStream. Internally SkCodec works with SkStream (the SkData interface is just a convenient wrapper) but for some reason SkCodecImageGenerator only takes SkData, so onRefEncodedData currently assumes that it can return an SkData. I realize this is an issue with the existing API, but ugh.

Not to mention that most of the time SkCodec appears to already have the fStream (though not always).

subject: Add SkCodec API to preserve original data
message: Also, this appears to force one to decode to get the the image in order to set this data, which seems to defeat the purpose of SkImage_Lazy (to not decode unless needed)?

subject: Add SkCodec API to preserve original data
message: For example if we call `refEncodedData` multiple times and get here, there will be multiple copies made, which at least didn't happen before (in which case there was actually only one copy of the data, since SkCodecImageGenerator enforced that it was a SkData and the codec lived off a stream wrapped around that data).

subject: Add SkCodec API to preserve original data
message:
In other words the "flatten to data" bit could be deferred to here for now, and eventually fix this to return a unique_ptr<SkStream> as well. Also for now this could cache the SkData in an fData here, which would be very inexpensive for SkData backed streams and possibly a big win for other streams (so we wouldn't need to keep making copies, though possibly also a loss if this isn't called again). Or do that caching in SkCodec for now.

On the other hand, it might just be best to add the stream based API as a separate thing and then remove this arbitrary reliance on contiguous data.

subject: Add SkCodec API to preserve original data

subject: Creating named instances for each variation in a variable font
message:
This `MakeFromStream` always makes a copy of the data (it should be updated to just return a reference to the data if it is a memory stream). Before we were "just copying twice" and now copying some arbitrary number of times. (FreeType doesn't make a copy, but calling FT_Open_Face isn't free either.) This should be avoided.

The easiest way to fix this would be to make the font scanner stateful, having a call to setup the data and then make calls against that. However I'd like to avoid that and instead turn `scanFile` into a factory function which returns a `SkFontFileScanner` which can hold onto the `FT_Face` in the FreeType implementation or the `SkData` in the Fontations implementation. Then `scanFace` and `scanInstance` can be on the `SkFontFileScanner` and not take the `stream` argument.

Of course at that point... `scanFace` is basically returning a whole default SkTypeface, except that SkTypeface won't tell you how many named instances there are.

subject: Make contrast calculation mimic DWrite on Windows
message:
This change should probably end up being the contrast adjustment on all platforms, there is no good reason to attempt to use different ones on different platforms (it will need to be rolled out behind a flag though). This particular calculation hasn't changed since it was introduced in https://codereview.appspot.com/6244068/diff/52002/src/core/SkMaskGamma.h#newcode105 (only eight years ago now).

The existing calculation is "plot (-c*a^2 + c*a + a) a = 0 to 1 c = 0 to 1". In this calculation c is limited from 0 to 1, as above 1 it could return values greater than 1, which would quite bad. This means that the existing calculation is limited in the amount of boost provided to lower alpha values to ~doubling their values. 

The proposed contrast calculation here is "plot (c*a + a) / (c*a + 1) a = 0 to 1 c = 0 to 4" which does what one would expect, as 'c' increases lower 'a' are boosted more. As c grows 0 stays at zero but every other value of a will tend towards 1. This provides opportunities for more coverage.

As a comment on coverage in general it is covering for two issues.

The first is pixel density and anti-aliasing. If a one pixel wide stem happens to end up on a half pixel boundary, even if all the blending is correct and the right number of photons get emitted from the display, the fact that the signal is over twice the area of a stem which is on a pixel boundary makes things look weird, so to compensate, do it more. (And often if the blending isn't right and the wrong number of photons are being emitted by the screen, some amount of 'do it more' may help compensate).

The second is just optical sizing. At smaller optical sizes it is expected that a greater percentage of the area will be covered relative to larger optical sizes. Increasing contrast by manipulating the mask is essentially the same as making all outlines a bit bigger by some amount of a pixel (in a weird hinted way). The percentage difference due to alpha contrast adjustment will be much higher for smaller renderings than larger ones, so while the same thing is done to both small and large the effect is much more noticeable on the small sizes. Note that on macOS this is done via 'font smoothing' which works on the outlines. The outlines are outset some amount with the outset determined based on the size (as a declining percentage of the size, used to just be a percentage of the size which looked really bad). This takes care of the optical sizing issue without adjusting the alpha values and messing with correct blending. (Note that on macOS 'font smoothing' also enables root two blending, without it incorrect perceptual blending is used which generally provides some 'contrast'.)

Note that all of this GAMMA stuff is a hack and so exposing it at all is less than ideal. When it was originally added the idea was that eventually the blitters would correctly blend the masks and we wouldn't need to be aware of this. The idea that the text would be in a different destination color space from everything else is an unfortunate one, mostly kept alive by it being set too low for the optical sizing effect (black on white text with a lower gamma looks much heavier at small pixel sizes due to over covered pixels) and it is hoped that variable fonts and automatic optical sizing will reduce the need for that.

Note that comments like https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=534732#c42 aren't about this, the difference there is the difference between using the v35 vs v40 (or newer) hinting engine. On the other hand we should probably investigate https://fontgammatest.netlify.app/ independently since it isn't immediately obvious what's happening there.

4. I'm aware of what the font does and what they're testing (#BCBCBC is close to 50% gray in srgb). However, a lot more is actually needed to separate out how the different renderers (Skia, FreeType, DirectWrite, CoreText) actually handle the tiny bits of coverage in that font to begin with, then with how the various back-ends (software, gpu) actually render through those coverage masks and also how users (in this case Chromium) have Skia configured. We would need particular tests at each level to know where things are different. It had previously been hoped that this would get fixed with the color space work, but it didn't really because the world is too dependent on blending non-linear things with linear blending.

subject: Add text gamma/contrast to SkSurfaceProps
message:
I'm a bit concerned about making this a public API like this. The reality is that this describes a colorspace. It just happens that some drawing APIs (like on Windows) expose a different color space for drawing glyphs and everything else.

So why isn't the existing colorspace on SkSurfaceProps? Well, it is on SkImageInfo (through SkColorInfo) since one needs to know how to draw out of it. On the other hand SkSurfaces don't really have a colorspace (the target may be deferred). Under the hood one can try to get at the colorspace by getting the SkCanvas and calling SkCanvas::imageInfo (which may come back without useful information, what is the colorspace of an skp or an nway canvas?). The colorspace information gets pushed through the Make* calls down to the internal SkDevices. I think that's somewhat seen here where this information needs to get set down on the device. As a result this may be more of a thing that gets passed as a separate colorspace to the Make* calls than living on the SkSurfaceProps.

In any event, I need to think about this a bit more to see if there is a cleaner way to express this sort of thing.

subject: Add text gamma/contrast to SkSurfaceProps
message:
The fact that on Windows the gamma and contrast are a per-monitor property is a very strong argument that not only should this global not go in a library it shouldn't be a single global (which is also an argument for why these existing globals which could vary on a per-monitor basis shouldn't be here as well).

I'm well aware that this makes the change in Chromium more difficult; while I've started on it twice I still haven't been able to get these globals out of Skia. All of these values need to come from the Display (ui/display/display.h) in Chromium (just like the color space) and be plumbed down to SkSurface creation. (Most of the issue with the existing globals, however, is moving all the existing surface geometry detection code which is all over the place around while keeping things working. Hopefully this proposal doesn't have that limitation and you can just pass the information down with the color space.)

Now, I don't really like the idea of the SkSurface having a different color space for text vs everything else, but I'll leave the prospect of adding another color space to SkSurface up to the owners of SkSurface. However, if these globals are added they will always be wrong and will be here for a very long time and Chromium will be unlikely to ever set the correctly. If you really want globals for pragmatic reasons that could better be done pragmatically in Chromium directly and let Chromium handle the technical debt of that (though I would much rather see this plumbed from Display on down).

subject: SkDynamicMemoryWStream::write: allow malloc to fail
message:
It's unfortunate that we haven't already considered what the state on failure should be. For instance, what happens if the user calls `write`, and this writes some in the tail, but allocating the next block fails? Should the write partially succeed? (If they tried writing again later, should that make sense?) In other words, should a failed write be atomic or should it leave the stream in an undefined but destructable state?

To support the atomic write, the logic of this needs to be essentially reversed from "if we have a tail then put some data into it, then get a new block and write the rest into that" to "first ensure that we have all the allocations we need to do this write, then do the writing". It isn't clear if that is really necessary here since most callers I can think of would simply discard this stream on write failure.

subject: SkDynamicMemoryWStream::write: allow malloc to fail
message: Heh, Skia doesn't even return a `size_t` like `fwrite` to indicate partial writes. So in practice `SkFILEWStream::write` already has the behavior that when returning false the buffer may have been partially written to the stream. So that's already in an undefined but destructable state. It seems unfortunate, but I suppose that's the precedent so far.

subject: SkDynamicMemoryWStream::write: allow malloc to fail
message: The issue is that this states too early that we've written so many bytes before the tail, but we haven't actually added the next block yet. It isn't correct to do this accumulation after the next block has been appeneded.

It looks like this is defined with storage in `SkDebug_android.cpp` which is provided by `//src/ports:skdebug` which is referenced in `//src/ports:srcs` (old build) and `//src/ports:base_srcs` (new build). This file is in `//tools/testrunners/common:testrunner` which deps on `//:core` which does deps on `//src/base:base`. message:
Chromium for Android complains that this is a global with a `CAPITALIZED_NAME` (or a `kCamelCaseName`) but it is in `.data` and not `.rodata`. This is because `SkMatrix` has a mutable field `fTypeMask`. While this object's `fTypeMask` isn't going to change, nothing prevents it being changed (it wouldn't be UB to change it) so it can't go in `.rodata`. The default constructor for `SkMatrix` is `constexpr` so this object should be constructed in `.data` at compile time, but it won't be write-protected.

This can be alleviated by naming it something else, like `identity`. Though it would be nice if SkMatrix didn't have hidden mutability.

Easy enough to fix forward with a rename, however there is a desire to cherry-pick this change into Chromium 122. The best course for now is to revert and re-land.

subject: Revert^2 "[Fontations-backend] Add COLRv0/v1 support to Fontations backend"
message:
After taking another look into this, I think I see the issue you're running into. cxxbridge does not allow any rust types defined outside the `ffi`, so there is no safe way to push `skrifa::color::ColorStop` over to the C++ side because we're writing the ffi Skia side instead of skrifa side. Hence the unsafe part of this isn't (as I originally thought) about passing a pointer and length over to Skia (which should be a `rust::Slice`) but about about directly casting a `&[skrifa::color::ColorStop]` to a `&[fontations_ffi::ColorStop]`. This issue in cxxbridge seems to be discussed at https://github.com/dtolnay/cxx/issues/1077 (and 670).

Since we are Skia side it looks like we could push what `populateStopsAndColors` does (plus the associated resizes which want the size) over to the rust side of things. In fact, since the first thing all these `fill_*` do is call `populateStopsAndColors` it seems like there isn't a need for a callback, the rust side could just make some vectors of Skia types and pass ownership of them over. It seems this might require something like `cxx::CxxVector` though that's also going to be an opaque type anyway (all access will go through calls).

So the only way I see to make this work without unsafe would be to keep this `fontations_ffi::ColorStop` but provide an opaque type wrapper around the slice (with a `usize size()` and `fontations_ffi::ColorStop get(i)`) or slice iterator (`Option<fontations_ffi::ColorStop> next()`) or something like that. Yes, this does mean a function call to get each value and a copy to make the return, but it does mean not making a full copy all at once (though that's actually not so bad since we're making more or less a full copy Skia side already).

I would rather take this rather modest perf hit (but with no extra heap allocations) than have to deal with the unsafe blocks in perpetuity.

subject: refactor freetype common into utils
message:
Ewwwww... I suppose I noticed this here first because now this takes neither a `FT_Face` nor an `SkGlyph`.

The statefulness of FreeType biting once again. In the new `generateGlyphPath` there just so happens to be another pointer to the same `FT_Face` as `fFace` which will, by action-at-a-distance, happen to have the same `glyph` loaded up. Of course, this pointer is being passed here through the implicit `this` pointer being passed. But the `this` is invisible and its `fFace`'s relationship to the `fFace` here is also invisible. It's a lot of invisible.

This is also an issue for all but the COLRv0/1 calls, since at least those don't have all this state on the FreeType side (the fact that SVG does is a real pain). For all the others there are hard pre-conditions on the state of the `FT_Face` before they can be called. This was already ugly before but somewhat unavoidable due to FreeType, but at least it was obvious that the `fFace` was being passed in and that its state is part of the call. Now it seems much more difficult to reason about, especially for what we would hope to be generally useful utility functions.

It might work to remove the `FT_Face fFace` from this SkScalerContext and instead use `fUtils.fFace` instead? That seems somewhat awkward, but at least would remove the awkwardness of needing to remember that there are two `fFace` pointers that need to be the same in order for anything to work. In other words, these two `fFace` pointers cannot just be pointing to the same logical `FT_Face`, they actually need to be pointing to the same `FT_Face` with the same internal state. The foreground color and flags don't have this issue since their entire state is in their value.

subject: refactor freetype common into utils
message: Of course the other way to do this is to just keep passing the `FT_Face` to each function directly. It seems awkward that it can be "factored out" to the class, but logically it's really difficult to think of it that way since the only part that is "factored out" is the pointer value but not large amount of state behind that pointer.

subject: [Fontations-backend] Add COLRv0/v1 support to Fontations backend
message:
The way to think about the scaler context bits is that they are the storage area for your "subclass" of `SkGlyph`. We don't want a bunch of subclasses of `SkGlyph` because that gets messy fast and we want them all to be the same size for storage reasons. However, each logical subclass of `SkGlyph` does need somewhere to put some state, mostly to cache scaler context specific information computed in `generateMetrics` to later calls (at the moment this is mostly "what format did I settle on?").

As a result, feel free to use this bits however makes sense. At the moment you're kinda using the "please create from path" bit to get the metics from path, but you'll probably want to have an enum value for that and call `GenerateImageFromPath`.

subject: Allow MSVC "host" builds
message:
Yes, I had to re-read through the docs again myself. If you're building for the default toolchain then things work as written in the gn files (in fact, the default toolchain's `toolchain_args` isn't evaluated, which can lead to interesting differences between using a toolchain explicitly and using it as the default). When building for a non-default toolchain the `toolchain_args` is used to override various things (usually just the built-in `current_cpu` and `current_os` like here).

From gn's perspective, "host" is where gn runs, "target" is what the default toolchain builds for, and "current" is what the current toolchain builds for.

message:
And a `TODO` here. SkParagraph should very not care about the SkUnicode implementation that it uses. And it shouldn't care which SkShaper it gets. Currently I think it might be creating them from the `Make` that cannot exist in the future to get whatever is compiled in, but really it should be sure to take these as input from the application  (it may already, would need to look to see). So as a result a name like `skparagraph_harfbuzz_icu` is really hard to look at. I realize this is "temporary" in the sense that its easy to do right now, but it is a big step backward in terms of the abstraction we're attempting to impose.

In other words, another really good reason to create `skshaper_module` and `skunicode_module` targets is that this is what this should depend on (after removing the generic `Make` factory) and then this code fixed up to work with that reality.

In other words, this change is doing a lot of "make a modular build" by pushing the "non-buffet" g3 build down here. Which is maybe ok temporarily, but just having this here tempts everyone into thinking this might be workable.

So maybe also a TODO on the name itself, pointing out that it is a really bad smell.

subject: Add Bazel buffet builds for paragraph and accessories
message:
Yes, it's a lot of work, and I'm not even sure it should block the build changes here, which are really just reflecting the actual state of the code (the idea of the code, like the rest of Skia, was to just build in the parts you want which isn't compatible with building modular pieces). In any event, I really just wanted a TODO here so that no one thinks this is all intentional or desirable (and which parts aren't intentional or desirable). For the moment this naming may even be correct and is pointing out a problem, I just want to be sure that we document here that it is a problem.

This is a general issue everywhere. In an unrelated change over in PDF, PDF has a dependency on SkJpegDecoder, but it really shouldn't and should have a jpeg decoder passed in somewhere so that it isn't depending on that specific decoder. To get around the possibility that this specific decoder wouldn't be present at build time it has it's own (optional at build time) mini-decoder that has no dependencies and reads the data directly. This leads to the issue that now there is yet another partial decoder. If something needs to be a configurable dependency then that just needs to be passed in by the user.

subject: [pdf] Emit color space of images
message: Directly depending on the decoder like this is very nice. However, it is awkward in the sense that it means always depending on this particular decoder, and doesn't allow the use of `SkJpegInfo_none.cpp` which is actually a minimal header reading only codec itself (except that it would need ICC parsing added to work with this).

subject: [pdf] Emit color space of images
message:
The alternatives are:

1. Keep `SkGetJpegInfo` and add an icc output parameter. The implementation in `SkJpegInfo_libjpegturbo.cpp` could be updated to use `SkCodec` (as is done here) and `SkJpegInfo_none.cpp` could be updated to parse out the icc profile or just return nullptr. Just extending this existing solution has the downside of being a build selected alternate which we are trying to get away from.

2. Do what is right here, just make pdf always depend on `SkJpegDecoder`. It appears all current users of pdf also depend on this codec anyway. However, it is a little awkward if the user doesn't otherwise need a jpeg decoder or has their own.

3. Allow a `SkCodecs::Decoder` to be passed in (on `Metadata`?). This is awkward because it would need to be a jpeg decoder (or at least a jpeg header decoder) and not something else, otherwise very surprising things might happen. Also, if they don't pass one in (which may be easy to miss) then this optimization can't happen, and it is fairly important.

subject: [pdf] Emit color space of images
message: At patch set 10 option 2 has been taken and PDF now directly depends on the JPEG decoder and encoder. These can be made optional and configurable in the future if needed.

subject: [pdf] Emit color space of images
message:
The encoder has the same issue. In `serialize_image` there is a direct call to `SkJpegEncoder::Encode`. This may be backed by an implementation in either `SkJpegEncoderImpl.cpp` or `SkJpegEncoder_none.cpp`, yet another build time selector. So if the jpeg decoder should be passed in, the encoder should be as well. Also, it appears that the current `src/pdf/BUILD.bazel` doesn't know about the encoder dependency.

This goes further, since there is a long standing request to be able to pass in a subsetter (though that is a larger and less stable interface making it more difficult to abstract).

subject: Revertng the revert of  "Emoji font resolution fix"
message:
If you have text with bunch of emoji, then creating the storage for this vector will be a lot of tiny allocations. Also, the only information this vector contains which the caller does not already know is the location of the end of the run of emoji. In other words, this method could just return `const char*` which points to the end of the emoji run (which would be equal to the initial value of `*begin` at the beginning of this function if there is no run of emoji). In fact, this is what `begin` is updated to anyway.

It would be much faster to just let `defaultEmojiFallback` take a span and let it iterate over the span (using `nextUtf8Unit`) than it is to allocate vectors like this.

subject: Revertng the revert of  "Emoji font resolution fix"
message:
If this takes a `begin**` and `end*` like this, then there is no need to (rather confusingly) also return an `SkUnichar`. Instead, this should just move `*begin` to the end of the current emoji sequence (which means not moving it at all if there is no emoji sequence) and then the caller can hold onto the "old begin" pointer and compare it to `*begin` after this call and see if they are different.

Alternatively, this could just return a `bool` for if an emoji sequence was found (implicitly meaning that `*begin` has changed).

Either way the caller would know the range based on the old value of `*begin` and the new value after calling this.

subject: Saturate glyph bounds
message:
So for a completely different take. Now, instead of having the SkScalerContext implementations handle saturating int32_t and having SkScalerContext itself take that and saturate the glyph bounds, just have the SkScalerContext implementations return floats (SkRect) and let SkScalerContext handle saturating the glyph bounds.

The nice thing about this is that there are fewer things that can go wrong (all the saturation code is in one place), it isn't any bigger (SkRect and SkIRect are the same size), the SkScalerContext implementations mostly need to use floats anyway (either because the values are reported in floats or because the values need to be mapped through a matrix), and we don't really lose precision because floats have 23 bits of integers which is more than the 16 we're going to saturate to anyway, so there's no loss when the SkScalerContext implementations need to round out and outset a fixed number of pixels for subpixel anti-aliasing. 

The downsides are that all the SkScalerContext implementations do need to be updated (though that should just be Skia and one outside implementation) and because I changed all this I need a new +1. So far I haven't seen any tests fail from doing this, though it's possible that in edge cases we may get slightly different rounding since there are now generally fewer roundings.

subject: Saturate glyph bounds
message: Maybe it might make more sense to just let this be an `SkRect` and then do the saturation just in `internalMakeGlyph`? That also mostly simplifies the scaler context implementations and fixes the edge cases where they round out but then add one for subpixel antialiasing (which they could just do in float anyway, since if there is an issue with adding 1 then the bounds are too big and unlikely to be correct to within 1 anyway).

subject: Add SkFontMgr to SkFontConfigInterface::makeTypeface
message:
This is a bit heavy. What this really wants is a `sk_sp<SkTypeface> (*make)(std::unique_ptr<SkStreamAsset>, const SkFontArguments&)`? Of course, that's kinda what this function was. This probably shouldn't even be a parameter to this function but a thing that is passed in to the constructor of the the `SkFontConfigInterface` instance. Which of course means not having the silly globals of this (`RefGlobal`, `SetGlobal`).

In other words, Chromium's `FontLoader::makeTypeface` should just use the `mgr` that would be passed here to just create the font. This `makeTypeface` would be pure virtual, and `SkFontConfigInterfaceDirect`'s constructor should take a factory function to call to create typefaces from (just like eventually all of our SkFontMgr will need to be able to do for other reasons). Of course the issue with this is `SkFontConfigInterfaceDirect` is created as a global! Globals everywhere! Need to get all of that out into Chromium instead of being in Skia first before anything sane can happen.

Anyhow, since nothing sane can happen anyway, this seems fine to me I guess.

subject: Make default typeface return empty
message:
In general, PortableTypeface should only be used in gms and when the text is a label (not logically part of the gm image under test). It can also be used if the intent really is to use the portable typefaces as a way to test something very specific (we don't think we would get code coverage testing with any native fonts), but this is pretty rare.

In general, I find it too easy to slap "PortableFont" onto things to try to make them more deterministic instead of getting real coverage and fixing issues. The reality is that no one sees any of those portable fonts but Skia developers, but a few billion people a day are looking at some of the default system fonts.

I'm sure I haven't quite reviewed all the uses here yet, will take another look later. Also, while Skia has pretty good test coverage, the organic way that coverage has grown turns into a lot of tests which don't seem to be covering much, but might be the one that covers some odd case, so it's really difficult to clean them up.

subject: Add new SkTypeface APIs which take SkFontMgr
message:
Unfortunately the term "fallback" with fonts means finding a fallback font for glyph coverage, which makes this name a bit misleading, even though it is accurate. This SkFontMgr is used as a kind of default factory function for data if the requested factory isn't present (which can lead to rendering issues, should probably be a warning about that somewhere) and is used if the data wasn't embedded (just go lookup the font by name, which generally also is broken and should be at least a warning).

So in the end this SkFontMgr can only produce incorrect results. The idea is that if the factory function isn't present then we should just return an empty typeface which draws nothing (and possibly tell the user that they have an invalid picture) but if you pass in this extra SkFontMgr then we will instead try desperately to find something that might match as a kind of last ditch effort to make something work (and maybe this SkFontMgr knows something about the serialization and can look up the right thing by name anyway if the user provides it).

So the right name for this might be `desperationFontMgr`. Any time it is used you will probably get the wrong glyphs drawn (and if they're right it is totally by accident). But sometimes drawing something or getting lucky while debugging is better than drawing nothing at all.

subject: [pdf] Simplify filled paths
message: Should comment that this algorithm of testing the cross product of the previous and current vector could be way more numerically stable, but this matches what the `Convexicator` class does for consistency.

subject: [pdf] Simplify filled paths
message: So this doesn't quite work because `Simplify` has a bug. `Simplify` has an early inexpensive check to see if the path is convex. If it is then there isn't any need to simplify and the path can just be returned as-is. However, `SkPath::computeConvexity` has a special case and extra code to ensure that a path with no area made up of verbs that return to the starting point the way it came is considered "convex". This means that `Simplify` does not simplify these zero area paths to nothing as expected. What `Simplify` wants is a "strictly convex" check where when the `cross == 0` and `dot < 0` (going directly backwards) doesn't count as convex.

subject: [pdf] Simplify filled paths
message: I believe this is now solved (as of Patchset 3) by doing the existing convexity test and then (if it is convex) testing for the path being trivial (all contours have zero area) and returning the empty path if it is.

subject: [pdf] Simplify filled paths
message:
The actual behavior of `SkPath::computeConvexity` is a bit more subtle at the moment than what I described. For example the `Convexicator::BySign` call is not just an accelerator, it protects the following checks from paths with more than three points (or more than two lines) from backward segments changing direction (and classifying some concave paths as convex).

After considering many options, the fix may be to introduce  a `SkPath::isConvexDoubledBack()` or some such thing so that `Simplify` can change its early out convexity predicate to something like `path.isConvex() && !path.isConvexDoubledBack() && !path.isEmpty()`.

However, the deserialize proc cannot call `DeferredFromEncodedData` without making a copy of the data since it takes a pointer and a length. There is no way for it to turn that into a sharable SkData without making a copy. Now, this may have already been an issue, because I assume that the deserialize proc usually needs to call out to the image decoders? I don't understand what the ownership rules of this data actually are here, so it is difficult to tell if it's actually possible for the user to write valid code to write an image proc to do this.

subject: Make SkReadBuffer *not* call SkImages::DeferredFromEncodedData by default
message: Yeah, this is already an issue because all the Chromium deserial procs all just `SkData::MakeWithoutCopy` on the data passed and then call the decoders with that SkData, even though they don't own the data. `MakeWithoutCopy` was (and is documented) to be used only with global data (where there is no allocation to free) and when you really know that the SkData cannot outlive the underlying data. All deserial procs in Chromium violate this and have ownership issues.

subject: [graphite] Switch signed unique ID iterators to unsigned.
message:
Well, signed overflow is UB, so leaving them signed means that if you overflow you may start WW3. Internally G3 is full of bad advice about signed vs unsigned. Also, these also aren't numbers but ids, so the actual representation hardly matters. If I could wave my magic wand I would insist that these not be `uint32_t` or any other "modular integer arithmetic type" but instead a "modular permuted bit identifier type" from which one could get the next permutation but nothing else (no +, -, *, /, implicit conversion to any arithmetic type, etc). In other words, since you asked, there is no reason for these to be signed, but there are reasons why it shouldn't be signed or unsigned.

Anyhow, at least this is less confusing with less UB than before. If only we had a good language to program in.

subject: Expand //:core and introduce //:png_decode_codec et al
message:
As pointed out by the G3 roll attempt, I don't see where this filegroup is ever used, even though `src/core:legacy_draw_looper` (the source filegroup) is.

That `filegroups` don't have `deps` (as `source_sets` in gn do) is absolutely disastrous and makes me doubt the suitability of bazel as whole (and reinforces my opinion that bazel is a nice dependency tracker, it would be nice if someone could write a build system on top of it). The fact that `//include/effects:public_hdrs` contains `SkBlurDrawLooper.h` in its list but no mention anywhere that it depends on this `legacy_draw_looper` target is completely unmaintainable.

This is a general issue that has been allowed to slide while we try to piece together a way to create a bazel build. But this is rapidly becoming an issue that needs to be addressed. We cannot have a build where we burry a bunch of filegroups in sub directories but then the upper levels need to magically know what their dependencies are. At that point there is no reason to have the filegroups in subdirectories at all because it's all just a big ball of mud and the "abstraction" is not providing any positive value but is simply hiding the cost of the missing information.

subject: Expand //:core and introduce //:png_decode_codec et al
message: Why are these listed here? You cannot usefully just build these (unless the target is explicitly already pose ssse3 or hsw). Same with other `_opts_` in here.

subject: Expand //:core and introduce //:png_decode_codec et al
message: How so? This file `SkBitmapProcState_opts_ssse3.cpp` does a `#define SK_OPTS_TARGET SK_OPTS_TARGET_SSSE3` and then includes a bunch of files which will change based on that. But then that list includes must be marked as textual headers since they will be compiled differently by different files (unless this is the only file in which they are included, in which case we should no longer set the define and that should all be inlined). I see no way to cleanly build this file in this list.

subject: Expand //:core and introduce //:png_decode_codec et al
message: Ugh... I can't even reason about this (and the the empty `textual_headers` in the new `:hsw`). It would take me all day. If they're not in `textual_headers` then (at least in g3 with their weird module system) each of the headers will get pre-compiled the first time they are used. But there are rules about how they are compiled when cached which makes this difficult to reason about. I mean, the issue here is that we're building a separate version of Skia in general for a different architecture than what we're actually targeting, but we're shoving into the same binary as the Skia for the "base" architecture. (We're really creating a fat binary, but doing so ourselves to avoid being super fat.)

subject: Validate FreeType COLR glyph data
message:
I don't think so. I would prefer to attempt to fallback to some other glyph representation if the COLRv1 data for a glyph for some reason isn't valid or understood. The issue really is that the FreeType side doesn't do any validation up front, only while traversing, so just because we can get a clip box from FreeType doesn't mean that there is any valid COLRv1 Paint tree in there.

For outline loading FreeType loads the whole thing up and will give an error if the outline can't be loaded. For bitmaps unfortunately we don't appear to actually ensure the bitmap is valid. In the case of SVG the bounds are needed and are created by parsing ~all the data to ensure that it is valid (currently the code returns early if the SVG data isn't valid, but there's nothing left to fall back to at that point the way things are right now). For COLRv0 the code here should be a little more strict, currently FreeType ensures that all the data is there but does not up front check that all the glyphids and paletteids are in range up front, early aborting if something doesn't check out on an iteration, though we do get `num_layers` so we do know when early exit happens and should skip the COLRv0 in that case instead of just drawing the first bit. I'll make that change here as well.

All that being said, I would prefer a sanity check up front that the data is valid.

Yes. That being said, that's what all the caching is for. The reality is that there are currently five or so different iterators and on a sane system (not Android) that's all we will create. We are creating a new one to return each time (they have mutable state, so cannot share them) which is why there is the language check, but it will usually be a clone of one in the cache (which is a "new" but that's about it). The reality is that outside of a few tests I've never seen anyone change the language in a single shaping call.

That being said, we could also do somewhat better and set a language/break iterator pair on the shaper itself to have a cache of one iterator on the shaper object itself, so that multiple calls to the same shaper with the same language cache use the same one. However, that does mean holding onto the break iterator, I'm not sure how big that is.

While it seems we may not want a `std::any` style `any_cast`, `std::optional` uses `value` and `value_or` (which return references) because the idea is to model value semantics as opposed to pointer semantics (like `std::unique_ptr::get` which returns a pointer). On the other hand, an `any_cast` here could at least statically check that the type being cast to derives from `Base`, which would be useful if ever refactoring things in the future.

subject: Use pointers to avoid static variable destruction.
message:
Sure you can, just ref the object and leak the ref into the pointer. It's the same thing that's being done here.

I do hate purposefully introducing a leak (even if it shouldn't matter here). What this is really pointing out is that Skia is a bad library and has globals and no "library object" to hang "defaults" off of. Basically "RefDefault" is bad and we should feel bad for having it, but no one is willing to do the work to get rid of it.

Also, this is a marker in the code that we don't want the bitmap to mutate, but this practically unenforced. `SkImage`(`SkImage_Raster`), `SkBitmap`, and `SkPixelRef` never actually enforce any sort of immutability and just blindly const cast everywhere. subject: Make SkMask immutable, introduce SkMaskBuilder
message:
The caching mechanism here previously relied on creating invalid / empty states on the stack, passing in a pointer, and have the "returned" object constructed down in the callee. This change cleans this up by doing that with `SkTLazy` to make it super clear that we're actually constructing these once (instead of a rather confusing amount of mutation).

This should probably be done by returning the value, but for the sake of changing as little as possible I'm using `SkTLazy`.

These changes to use `SkTLazy` appear to be responsible for all of the code size increase in this change. It isn't clear why that is since everything here is in headers and should just all inline to about the same (or even less) code.

subject: Fix DirectWrite port COLRv1 clang warnings
message:
Direct3D 10 and later reference documentation only documents "new" things and not the entire interface. Since `D3DCOLORVALUE` isn't new (just changed from d3d9 and earlier) it isn't documented in the Direct3D 10 and later documentation. However, it is different and the difference should have been documented. So I can say for certain that the documentation linked at the start of this thread (about direct3d9) is out of date (unless you're using d3d9). `D3DCOLORVALUE` is now (since d3d10) four unions, it just isn't documented anywhere except in the headers themselves.

That being said, while `dxgitype.h` should probably be fixed I don't think we need to worry about it accidentally being included here. This is part of dxgi which is kind of the user mode part of the direct3d graphics driver. Nothing in these files should ever be pulling in that header.

However... note that this Makefile uses `wget` directly against `www.unicode.org` to get the Unicode data. We really cannot be doing this (and it reflects somewhat poorly on libgrapheme for doing so) as it is not really reproducible. Sure, the Unicode consortium states that it won't change these files once they are published, but these files can also just go away for various reasons (they have the same problem as us not having a local mirror of libgrapheme, only more so). These inputs would also need to be mirrored / checked in somewhere and the BUILD.gn use that (and not attempt to download files during the build). In a BUILD.bazel build it might be possible to version and cache these as if we were pointing at another repo (including checking hashes of the context), but even then for actual reproducibility reasons (and sanity reasons) to be building with a specific copy of these files.

subject: [Fontations] External factory for instantiating Fontations typeface
message:
SkFontMgr has `_factory.cpp` in order to facilitate a default SkFontMgr, but there are no `_factory.h` files because the actual `SkFontMgr_New_Foo` are in the `include/ports/SkFontMgr_foo.h` headers. So in theory this should be `SkTypeface_fontations.h`, but Skia wants all the header names to be unique, so that doesn't work, does it? The other ports get away with it by the public headers being more generic (and possibly less well named), like `include/ports/SkTypeface_win.h` as the public header and `src/ports/SkTypeface_win_dw.h` as the internal header name.

I'd hate to create yet more churn on this CL, but one Chromium starts using this file it will be more difficult to rename. I feel like this public header should get the "better" name of `SkTypeface_fontations.h` and maybe the internal one in `src/ports` should be `SkTypeface_fontations_priv.h` or something (I really dislike the `impl` and `priv` things, but visibility in headers is silly).

subject: [Fontations] External factory for instantiating Fontations typeface
message:
I'd complain about the inconsistency of this name, but we're already so inconsistent that making it consistent with anything else would be inconsistent at this point. Though generally Skia tries to make all top level functions like this start with `Sk`. Maybe we should use the existing pattern on SkFontMgr (like `SkFontMgr_New_Android`) and name this function `SkTypeface_New_Fontations`. Though maybe breaking with that and being `SkTypeface_Make_Fontations` would be more consistent with the `Make` terminology used in SkTypeface?

Skia started out with `Create` everywhere, but those all returned raw pointers because it was all C++03. To have a different name when updating to smart pointers `Make` was the replacement. But early on some things used `New`. So now there is a mix of `Create`, `Make`, and `New`. An English thesaurus is quite thick.

subject: Attach an ellipsis to the end of a grapheme
message:
You may want to reconsider the name and ensure it is the new behavior which is behind a flag, not the old (otherwise there will be extra steps when removing the flag). The issue here is that when `SK_SKPARAGRAPH_ELLIPSIS_BEHAVIOR` is defined you will get the new behavior (and get the old behavior if it is not set). This is the opposite of what is intended.

I would recommend a flag name like `SK_IGNORE_SKPARAGRAPH_ELLIPSIS_FIX` to make it obvious that using this flag disables a fix in behavior. Then this looks like

```
#ifdef SK_IGNORE_SKPARAGRAPH_ELLIPSIS_FIX
    if (!fTooLongWord || hasEllipsis) {  // Old, avoided grapheme ellipsis
#else
    if (!fTooLongWord && !hasEllipsis) {  // New, allows grapheme ellipsis
#endif
```

That way Skia is testing the new behavior and when no user is setting `SK_IGNORE_SKPARAGRAPH_ELLIPSIS_FIX` the ifdef (and any comments) here can be removed.

subject: Require std::has_unique_object_representations for SkGoodHash
message:
This seems like a dangerous operation in general, since K is not necessarily densely packed. There are no guarantees about what happens to the padding, even if you allocate and zero the memory, the padding is up for grabs and writes are allowed to it (which would of course upset the hash). The most common case of this is on little endian machines if there is a "small" last field but known "large" padding where writes may be to the "large" to avoid a masking operation.

Even if you do a loop here and allow each K to hash itself and write a "hash combine" (which would at least create deterministic hash, assuming K has a deterministic hash) this is awkward as a general utility because the SkSpan doesn't own or control any of the K it is referencing so wouldn't know when its own hash changed.

Generally having a hash of a container isn't something one wants as general utility. If any of the content changes then the overall hash is changed. Since the meaning is so heavily tied to whatever the implementation using this needs then how the span is hashed really should be a one off, or at least non-generic with a heavy name. For more arguments along these lines look up "why is there no std::hash<std::vector<T>>".

subject: Require std::has_unique_object_representations for SkGoodHash
message: That's true, but also ignores the larger issue that this should not be a generally available thing called "SkGoodHash" since it isn't a generally good hash since the object being hashed (the SkSpan) does not own the bits in the Ks and force them to be immutable. In other words, this is only a "good hash" if the caller can also guarantee that whatever owns the thing pointed to by the SkSpan is going to be immutable for as long as the hash is going to be interesting. Strings can get away with this since they are generally immutable (COW is disallowed on std:string, SkString is actually a bit iffy to be hashed).

subject: Add skia_public_no_copts target
message:
So there is `bazel/copts.bzl:DEFAULT_COPTS` which contains (among other things) `-fno-rtti` and `-fWerror`. Then this is set as the default list of `copts` in `bazel/macros.bzl:skia_cc_*`. So then this is essentially turning all of those off. This is more or less in an attempt to add a "is_official_build" like setting.

At the moment the Skia specific bazel build (the parts in `bazel/`) are more or less how a developer of Skia would want to build Skia. The idea seems to have been that if someone wanted their own build of Skia for any reason they would need to implement all of that for their own build (e.g. one cannot just change the toolchain without re-implementing the rest, since the rest kinda depends on the toolchain). This seems to be some sort of attempt to make the Skia build a bit more "flexible", but if that is the goal then that needs to go much further as `is_official_build` does, potentially requiring the user to provide their own hooks to any dependencies (use system libraries or their own versions of libraries or what have you).

message:
As a note to anyone here from the future, while it is interesting to keep everything valid premul (and that was possibly an issue at the time) allowing non-opaque subpixel rendering without per-channel alpha isn't very helpful. It looks fine for something that is like 90% opaque, but does not work well with blending onto a transparent black background to be composited onto another layer.

This is mostly because when the alpha picked for the whole pixel is larger than the coverage of the subpixel then the difference will be made up in black, making the subpixel too dark when blended into another layer (dark halo). If the alpha is less than the coverage of a subpixel then the coverage will essentially be clipped to the alpha when blended, leading to not enough coverage when blended into another layer (thin, blocky, not enough coverage).

If there is a reasonable guess at the color of the layer which will be blended into then one could do the dst blend against that color instead of the actual dst, hoping that works out. This is similar to just filling the current transparent layer with the guess at the destination color, but only on the pixels where subpixel antialiasing will happen. This can be made to kinda work, but looks bad when the guess isn't close.

subject: Fix alpha coverage for lerp_565 stage.
message:
or should this be max(lerp(da, a, cr), lerp(da, a, cg), lerp(da, a, cb)) ? These two give the same answer when a >= da, but when a < da these are different (in that case lerp(da, a, min(cr, cg, cb) would be equal to the max of the lerps).

For example, consider the case where a = 0.5, da = 1.0, cr = 0.75, cg = 0.5, cb = 0.4. Then

> lerp(da, a, max(cr, cg, cb))
> = (a - da)*max(cr, cg, cb) + da
> = (0.5 - 1.0)*0.75 + 1.0
> = 0.625

> max(lerp(da, a, cr), lerp(da, a, cg), lerp(da, a, cb))
> = max((a - da)*cr + da, (a - da)*cg + da, (a - da)*cb + da)
> = max((0.5 - 1.0)*0.75 + 1.0, (0.5 - 1.0)*0.5 + 1.0, (0.5 - 1.0)*0.4 + 1.0)
> = max(0.625, 0.75, 0.8)
> = 0.8

For example, the largest possible value of b is

> lerp(db, b, cb)
> = (b - db)*cb + db
> = (0.5 - 1.0)*0.4 + 1.0
> = 0.8

so lerping the max gives a value too small (no longer pre-multiplied) but the max lerp should give a pre-multiplied answer. I have no idea if this makes any physical sense, but middle pre-multiplied stages seem difficult to reason about.

subject: [pdf] Output drawable glyphs as XForms
message:
This turns out to be fairly straight forward to enable, but I have noticed that PDF doesn't actually compress all that well (even with gzip'ed streams) so this makes printing a fully expanded https://fonts.google.com/noto/specimen/Noto+Color+Emoji/glyphs printed to PDF go from 6.6MB to 15.7MB. However, this is more or less perfect for scaling and the existing bitmaps being used for COLRv0 and COLRv1 are actually produced with aliased rendering at a fairly small size (I think size 64).

In particular with a font like https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Cairo+Play this makes a big difference, as with this font )and without this change) the glyphs without any color draw from outlines and the glyphs with color are drawn with bitmaps, which is rather awkward looking sometimes.

In any event, may need to add some way to control the size maybe. Or maybe not. Will need to look more.

Current pdf.js does not support function shaders [0]. They do have a full interpreter which even has some optimizations, but it isn't hooked into the shader code. Skia is using these a lot for gradients which PDF otherwise doesn't support.

Preview appears to be getting some transform or clip box incorrect, and doesn't appear to be drawing or filling all of the contours in some cases. Will need to investigate that a lot more.

[0] https://github.com/mozilla/pdf.js/issues/5046

subject: [pdf] Output drawable glyphs as XForms
message:
Also wanted to point out here that SkPDFGradientShader#make_function_shader already does try to use PDF's built-in gradient support if it can. However, this can only be done in non-perspective and clamp tiling [0] (aka. pad extend [1,2], aka how css gradients work [3]) mode [4]. (In theory it looks like decal mode could also be supported, but it isn't used very often.) However, a number of ColrV1 fonts currently available (like Bungee Spice) default all their gradients to reflect extend mode. Even if the reflect is not seen, we do not attempt to analyze how the gradient will be used to notice if the extend mode doesn't matter and then lower to clamp/pad.

[2] https://www.w3.org/TR/2011/REC-SVG11-20110816/pservers.html#LinearGradientElementSpreadMethodAttribute
[3] https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html#interpolation

message:
These ones I happen to know are super lightweight, it's a library call which is just a getter on a field of the underlying `CTFontDescriptor`. This is really nothing compared to the silly overhead of getting at any bits in the `OS/2` table, where CoreText will make a copy each time a table is requested, and then Skia warps that in an SkData, so there are at least two dynamic allocations just getting the data. (Which is why this change goes out of its way not to access it twice.) Also, this is in getting the font metrics, which basically happens once when creating an SkTypeface.

On the other hand, almost all fonts do have these tables, so there's no reason not to factor these out.

subject: Use standard fast unsigned types instead of our own defined ones
message:
To be technically correct...

`a`, `r`, `g`, and `b` need to be cast to at least `SkColor` (`uint32_t`) before the shift operator is applied. If `uint_fast8_t` is smaller than `int` then the values will be promoted to `int` and the shift will be signed and produce a signed result and at least the shift of `a` might be undefined (shifting a set bit into the sign bit).

Even worse, `int` is allowed to be smaller than `uint32_t`, though most of Skia probably just wouldn't compile in that case. In which case the shifts would be undefined.

Of course, if `uint_fast8_t` happens to be larger than `SkColor` the casts would be pessimizing and we'd be better off without them. Of course, the optimizer should figure that out an emit good code anyway... but who knows. Really you want to cast to a type which is the bigger of `uint_fast8_t` and `SkColor`. subject: [skottie] Add shaper cluster info
message:
The name here is interesting, since even the comment says "glyph cluster information" but the field name is `kUTFClusters`. This is why in shaper this is just called `clusters`, since each cluster[i] is really a mapping from returned glyph[i] to the index of the start of the slice of the input string which caused that glyph to be produced. The values are indexes into the input string of code units, so I can see why this might be seen as "UTF Clusters" but the keys are indexes into the glyph array, so these are also glyph clusters (runs of the same value in the array). `startUtfIndexFromGlyphIndex` might be a better name (making it obvious that this is really a dense map, not just an array of values), though we tend to give that concept a name and call it `clusters`.

Anyhow, naming things is hard.

subject: [includes] Enforce IWYU on even more base files
message:
This always drives me crazy. Yes, in C++17 the C headers are deprecated, but when changing to the `<c*>` versions it is not guaranteed that the `<c*>` versions will put the declarations into the global namespace (they're only required to put them into the `std` namespace). It used to be that they weren't supposed to pollute the global namespace at all (only provide the `std` ones, like `std::size_t`) but C++17 now allows the practice of polluting the global namespace by default since all the major implementations did. 

Section D.5 of the C++17 spec (at least draft n4659).

[Example: The header <cstdlib> assuredly provides its declarations and definitions within the namespace std. It may also provide these names within the global namespace. The header <stdlib.h> assuredly provides the same declarations and definitions within the global namespace, much as in the C Standard. It may also provide these names within the namespace std. — end example ]

In other words, I don't really have an issue with using the `<c*>` versions, but that does mean that we should be using all of the declarations out of the `std` namespace.

subject: Remove unneeded SkTypes from base classes
message:
Well, for at least some of it, the build (gn, bazel, cmake, whatever). If there's something that should be defined for every translation unit then that should be set by the build. Things like `SK_BUILD_FOR_*`, `SK_CPU_ENDIAN`, `SK_CPU_X86`, `SK_CPU_SSE_LEVEL`, etc are currently set based on asking the compiler, but these should really be communicated from the build (they kinda are indirectly through the compiler, but that also means we need `SkTypes.h` included to get basic things instead of them just being provided). The nice part in favor of `SkTypes.h` though is that it means that someone using a different means of building Skia doesn't have to figure out all the defines to set. Basically, for almost any file where we include `SkTypes.h` by itself at the top to get a define and then `ifdef` out the rest of the file should have been handled by the build, and if we really needed the define that should come from the build as well and not from magically including `SkTypes.h`.

Other things like `SkDebugf`, the asserts, `SkTAlign*`, `SkSetFourByteTag`, the `Abs`, and such should probably be in a different header(s). This is just using `SkTypes.h` as a dumping ground for "small utils".

subject: Deprecate kStrokeAndFill
message:
Another argument for adding

    && !paint.getPathEffect()

is that if there is a path effect, the result may not actually end up being hairline (which is the issue SkScalerConetext used to have until recently). The "draw as path" code path currently works because when drawing from path the fill-only, no-path-effect version of the paint is used to get the "base path". (Note that this means the path effect is not cached, and will be applied to the path each time drawn.)

In fact, now that we handle hairline correctly in the SkScalerContext, I'm not sure why we bail on hairline here anyway. Sure, it may be somewhat quicker to draw a hairline path (is it?), but this means that hairline glyphs may be drawn from different (unhinted) outlines than the same text drawn without hairline, leading to gaps when doing hairline stroke over already drawn filled glyphs. Considering that drawing hairline glyphs is probably rare it seems that correctness may be more desirable than a potential speed up (have we actually measures this at any point?). It may be easier to just remove this hairline "optimization" from SkStrikeSpec::ShouldDrawAsPath.

In any event, this change still seems good to me for landing as-is. At least I understand why the one 'A' changed.

subject: Deprecate kStrokeAndFill
message:
So it appears that the reason why typeface_styling changed ever so slightly with this is that before (sSrokeAndFill) was drawn through the scaler context but now (Stroke) it is being drawn as a path (so a slightly different outline which may be hinted at a different size).

The reason for this is SkStrikeSpec::ShouldDrawAsPath which states if

    SkPaint::kStroke_Style == paint.getStyle() && 0 == paint.getStrokeWidth()

is true then it's hairline and shoudl be drawn as paths. However, this should probably add a

    && !paint.getPathEffect()

to this predicate since it's probably worth caching the path effect being applied to the hairline anyway. Indeed, if I add this, then the typeface_styling gm becomes unchanged.

message:
This seems like a fine organization (all these flags and defines really are part of Skia's build and not really a thing that needs to be overridden, since you "override" all of these with bazel flags). I'm not sure about the name `base_defines.bzl` though. I understand that it might be slightly confusing to have both a `//defines.bzl` and a `//bazel:defines.bzl` but that seems less odd to me. 

The awkward part really seems to be that the `//bazel/` part (or directory) is really a `//bazel_ext/` or something like that, where any user of Skia (including Skia) needs to put some (at the moment not very well defined) set of bazel definitions which define how to do certain things in that bazel environment (it's the customization point). As it is named now it looks like the place where general bazel build things go, but it isn't that anymore.

All that to say that the `base_` in `base_defines.bzl` seems a little redundant. If anything, this "base" one should be `//defines.bzl` and other one should be `//bazel:extra_defines.bzl` or `//bazel_ext:defines.bzl`. Of course, changing the name of the existing one there is more difficult.

subject: Make SVG/XML parsing only print errors in debug mode
message: Yeah, we shouldn't be using unguarded `SkDebugf` in release in general. We're a library so if we want to pass an error message back to the user that's fine, but as a library we shouldn't be doing global things like writing directly to stderr or stdout in release builds (or crashing if we can possibly avoid it, for that matter). The fuzzer is probably a good was for us to find these, since generally our tests don't test all these interesting failure cases. (I remember distinctly at least one release of CoreText which would write directly to stderr if it thought a particular matrix passed in was singular, even though that was fine and it actually handled that correctly. Very annoying to work around.)

message:
Building on Linux without this change like

```
is_debug = false
is_component_build = true
werror = true

skia_use_harfbuzz = true
skia_use_system_harfbuzz = true
skia_pdf_subset_harfbuzz = false

skia_use_system_freetype2 = true

skia_use_vulkan=true
```

```
ninja -C out/shared skia
bloaty out/shared/libskia.so -n 1000 -d compileunits -s vm
```
Shows that this produces a binary with VM size of 8.34Mi. This is contains the FreeType port, the FontConfig, Android, and Custom SkFontMgr. This does not include FreeType, HarfBuzz, or ICU.


Building again on Linux without this change like
```
is_debug = false
is_component_build = true
werror = true

skia_use_harfbuzz = false
skia_use_sfntly = false
skia_use_freetype = false
skia_use_icu = false
skia_use_vulkan=true
```

subject: aggressively reuse GrTextBlobs for non-subpixel-positioned blobs
message:
So the idea is that no matter how you move around pixel positioned bitmaps they're going to be the same bitmap. The actual locations of those bitmaps may need to be regenerated (the offsets between them may change), but the bitmaps themselves won't ever need to be regenerated.

We don't have 'subpixel bitmaps' (well, we kinda do with SDF, but we don't call them bitmaps here) so there isn't really any way to apply that logic to subpixel positioned things (without uploading the whole set of subpixel bitmaps and letting the shaders pick).

subject: Reland "[bazel] Add individual test targets, broken up by CPU and GPU"
message:
Because these flags are set here, all the `PDF_TESTS` are run against a different build (built from scratch) of all of `libskia_internal.a` (all source files appear to be recompiled from scratch, there appears to be no sharing, these are in `bin/_objs/skia_internal`). When building a test with a different set of flags there will be a separate directory under `bazel-out/` each with its own complete build of the objects listed in `libskia_internal.a` (in addition to it's own build of the sources from the test framework target and the tests themselves). I discovered this while attempting to run all of the tests and wondered why it was taking so long, and it turned out I had 9 complete builds of Skia.

In the gn build we've been building a maximalist everything included libskia build and running all enabled tests against that. This is doing things the other way around and stating that each set of tests builds the minimal libskia exactly as it needs it. This is a more bazel thing to do and is probably a better test to ensure that the dependencies are actually correct, but it's a lot of building. I realize that most will just say "well, distribute the build over more machines!" but Skia has many more of these optional bits to add to the tests and I have a general concern about doing more work than necessary.

With Android we have the follow on issue of every set of tests (currently per source test file) statically linking in `libskia_internal.a`, so usually at least ~8MB per test. In addition to that each one of these `skia_cpu_tests` with a different set of `flags` currently has a different `libskia_internal.a` so we cannot currently share those either.

[skottie] Fix range selector handling of empty lines
message:
Ok, that gets into asking what a "line" is (and why Shaper doesn't handle formatting). It depends on if you interpret `\r` as a "line break" or "end of line". I usually read it as a "line break" implying that there is a new line after it (even if empty). If it just means "end of line" then there is no new line until there is further content. What I see here is

line 1 ""
`\r`
line 2 ""
`\r`
line 3 ""
`\r`
line 4 "foo"
`\r`
line 5 ""
`\r`
line 6 ""

If it isn't interpreted this way then it seems rather awkward to have a last empty line if one wants one. It means adding a `\r\r` at the end to get one empty line to force the actual last line (or penultimate line?) to be "non-empty" by virtue of being "ended" by the actual final `\r`.

subject: [skottie] Fix range selector handling of empty lines
message:
So here you run into an empty line and send it off to the skottie shaper as an empty line. `shapeLine` the notices that this is empty and then calls `beginLine` and `commitLine`. The `commitLine` keeps track of the line count in `ResultBuilder::fLineCount`. (The line count was already being kept in the ResultBuilder.) `commitLine` when it outputs things (which creates fragments) passes along the current line so that the fragment is aware of the line it is on. This change then puts this `ResultBuilder::fLineCount` into the new `skottie::Shaper::Result::fLineCount`.

This change (at PS9) then uses this information by going over the fragments and adding in any lines missing, using `skottie::Shaper::Result::fLineCount` to know how many might be missing at the end.

I was going to suggest that maybe the when building the result that there be an extra `addEmptyLine` which could be called here which adds the empty fragment. I suppose that's a bit less performant since it would need to be created, but I think would simplify things since then there would be a fragment for every line.

Which subclass of SkScalerContext does this?

Even if they do, this returns the maximum of the glyphs that don't have a 0 size. If some glyphs are smaller and work and others are larger and get 0s then they won't be considered?


Currently SkGlyph only supports int16 top and left with uint16 width and height. If these limits are exceeded we do currently zero the metrics (it looks like all implementations now do this). So the max bounds should be more like (-32767, -32767, 65535, 65535), or something like that. If this is what's actually happening, maybe we need some kind of error code out of SkScalerContext::makeGlyph (maybe we could use a bit from SkGlyph::fScalerContextBits to indicate that the metrics are zero because they don't fit)? This would also allow to tell the difference between space glyphs that draw nothing for real and oversized glyphs that won't fit in SkGlyph.

If there's something else that's causing the metrics to get zero'ed (like the underlying library has limits) then we should know about that too and try to work around that (like the SkScalerContext subclass should get the largest size and scale up, we already have the mechanism in place in all of them to do that anyway).

subject: Use matrices instead of font size for controlling large glyphs
message:
The largest multiple between `.` and `M` isn't really limited, since the bounds can be pretty much anything especially with CFF outlines (everything is float). In practice this is generally limited to the range of a 26.6 (or 16.16) fixed point. The units per EM number is just what to divide by to get to a size of 1 (then multiply by the size you want), it's not actually a square anymore and nothing needs to fit inside it. So there's really no largest multiple that would really be safe here.

We've never really cared too much about what happens on size overflow before, but here we probably will, so yeah, we will need to plumb that information out of the scaler context and up. So long as we have an issue to track that and a TODO here I'm fine with this.
