subject: [bazel] Set up staged rollouts into G3 using defines.
message:
On the one hand I understand the desire for this as an option. However, if this is for staging Skia changes it's generally a better idea to set such defines in the target code repository (for these to be specified directly in G3). The idea is to be able to atomically remove the flag (making the Skia change appear) and fix up the target. To do this the flag must be removed in the target repository. Adding a flag here allows for suppression of the new code at the same time as the Skia side change, but then there will still need to be another change to also define the flag on the G3 side anyway, then a change to remove the flag from here, then a change on the G3 side to remove the flag there while updating the G3 code. Along the way it's also easy to end up in an awkward situation where both G3 and Skia are trying to set the same flag.

Staging flags like this in public.bazel were a bad idea too, and were never staging flags anyway. They were permanent flags that someone sometime might want to work on removing, so they were never "extra".

In short, I think making a place for such flags here is a bad idea. To the point where I would actually encourage this change with a G3 side change where the build asserts that EXTRA_DEFINES is empty with a big comment about how you did things wrong if it isn't.

subject: [includes] Enforce IWYU on src/images
message:
Oh, I see the issue is that SkJpegCodec implicitly declares an inline virtual destructor. (This requires any TU which includes it to generate a default implementation.) Instead, SkJpegCodec should declare its destructor (as override) and define it in SkJpegCodec.cpp.

Locally, declaring `~SkJpegCodec() override;` below and then adding `SkJpegCodec::~SkJpegCodec() = default;` (right after the constructor) to SkJpegCodec.cpp makes everything work out more nicely. The decoder target then correctly hides its implementation details, and iwyu correctly starts pointing out that JpegDecoderMgr needs only be forward declared. (And there's no need for any awkward build changes.)

There's no downside to doing any of this, since ~SkJpegCodec is already virtual. And there is the upside of the linker not needing to clean up the mess of all the generated destructors.

If it's GPU it's flaky. There's always some unrelated GPU flakes in there, and I leave that issue to the GPU team.

subject: [COLRv1] Use generated test descriptions
message:
I've skimmed the DirectWrite API and I don't even see any support for glyph names. Even the Skia PDF backend doesn't actually need them (as evidenced by not getting them most of the time) and the function should probably be removed from Skia since it cannot really be supported anymore. While COLRv1 support is currently FreeType only, it is expected to be supported elsewhere and I would expect any tests to also work correctly (even if just doing fallback) on all platforms. Indeed, I've found the COLRv1 test font insufficient due to the lack of fallback outlines in the past (not sure if that's been fixed or not yet).

I considered doing a material design font like design like you suggest, shaping stings into particular glyphs. However, it seems way overkill as well to drag shaping into this.

Why would the code points need to be shifted when adding new glyphs? These should probably all be mapped to PUA code points anyway just to be nice, though even if they were all just assigned low ascii compatible code points there's no reason to move them about. When adding a new glyph / code point to the test font I really do want there to be a corresponding change to the test itself to directly show that there is an intentional change to that particular test.

subject: [COLRv1] Use generated test descriptions
message:
More importantly, getting the glyph names is only really supported for Type1 fonts using the FreeType port. In theory it should work for OT fonts with FreeType, but nothing has every been implemented here for the DirectWrite and CoreText ports. I'm not even sure if they support this well.

It seems like the level of indirection needed here is just to map them in the cmap table so that you can use code points instead of glyph indexes? That would be a lot less crazy. This would generally mean not using std::regex and needing to specify all the codepoints to draw, but I think I would prefer that level of specificity. (The ColrV1GM constructor would just take a string to draw.)

message:
Yeah, this was the reason for https://skia-review.googlesource.com/c/skia/+/385516 (and not ANGLE is doing a similar thing). Everyone was polluting the global base targets and getting in each other's way. So instead we just "inherited" from those targets in our own "namespace" and then set configs on that (without using gn's `set_defaults`). Not sure if it's possible to make a skia_cc_library in Bazel, but that's effectively what this is trying to do, right?

Part of the issue is that really Skia is one huge monolithic build and isn't really made of separable components. If we wanted to reflect reality there really would be one giant `skia` target with a ton of conditionals in it for everything. However, that's difficult to manage so we pretend like there a multiple cc_libraries and whatnot, but the reality is that this doesn't reflect reality. So we end up with this interesting "all Skia sub-targets depend on this list of copts" because really that's the list of copts that the monolithic `skia` target would have. (This is true of both the gn and the bazel builds currently.)

subject: Mark sk_sp with [[clang::trivial_abi]] attribute
message:
After reading through all the things (the clang changes, the proposed C++ changes, the related chromium issue, and some other related suchlike) and all the caveats, the nice thing about `sk_sp` is that it fits in all the proposed categories so should be fine with any of the proposed annotations and any of their proposed semantics. The entire point of `sk_sp` is to be like `unique_ptr` where the "deleter" is to call unref, so anything that would work for `unique_ptr` should work here.

That being said, Skia does require C++17 which states that unknown attributes should never be errors. Can we just unconditionally mark this class with the attribute without all the macro mucking about? (At the very least reduced to what SkSpan is doing.) I would support just enabling this attribute since it's (almost) spec compliant (no one should be depending on the order `sk_sp` are created or destroyed in within an expression for side effects).

subject: [bazel] Add rules for CanvasKit and dependent modules
message:
Just as a more general note (and not to change anything here right now, more of a musing) `enable_fonts_true` is used four times here in four different selects. It is interesting how Bazel's setup really pushes toward slicing based on type of thing being set. `gn` was fine with this way if it was wanted, but also made it simple to slice based on predicate. For example in gn this would be more natural like `if (enable_fonts_true) { srcs+= defines+= flags+= deps+= }`. With Bazel the predicate is repeated and the logic of a given configuration dispersed. This is somewhat offset with forcing the predicate to be simple (just a name) so it can be easily searched for, but it is still spread around. On the other hand, gn spread the assignment to things around, sometimes making it difficult to determine for a given build configuration what the actual values would end up being and why. On the other hand, both systems have introspection to show for a given configuration what everything was set to in the end, and while editing build files I'm generally more concerned about the effect of a particular predicate than the end value of, say, all defines.

I suppose what I'm really saying is that if one wants to be entirely declarative, this is a table of things on one axis and predicates on the other axis, with each table cell being the values to append to the things when the given predicate is true. (This is of course very messy when one wants to remove a value if present, but this is still logically possible by further massaging of the predicates.) As such I wish there were a visual table format for this instead of trying to shove it into an arbitrary hierarchy just because we're stuck with a linear text only format.

subject: Fix the start/end indexes used for font features in SkParagraph
message: Features should not break runs. The way features are specified in OpenType is specifically so they don't break runs. Logically, on the input side features are specified as a property applied to each codepoint which is then applied to the default glyph it maps to and a feature is active at a given location if the current glyph has that feature set. (Indeed, in the implementation in HarfBuzz, the set of active features is a bitset associated with each codepoint/glyph in the buffer.) From the API side we express this as ranges because that's generally more compact than specifying the features explicitly for each codepoint. However, just because one codepoint has a different set of features than the previous codepoint should not break shaping (indeed, that would be counter to the idea of features).

subject: [canvaskit] Always serialize Typeface data into SKPs
message:
Typeface serialization is a mess, and I wish I had time to work on it and someone to actually review the changes I've made in the past to start working on it. The issue isn't so much at serialization time but deserialization. However, passing a fontmgr to the deserializer would be incorrect in the same way our current system is incorrect, in that it assumes that deserialized typefaces should be created with some default fontmgr (and there shouldn't even be a default fontmgr).

In the original issue, when the paragraph was created a custom fontmgr was passed to it for use. These typefaces were serialized with the intent that at deserialization the fontmgr that created them would be the default one. Deserialization knows nothing of this custom fontmgr which created these typefaces and attempts to use the default one. There is no failure mode, so the default fontmgr returns the one default font it has, which is obviously unrelated to the original fonts used.

The way one is supposed to handle this is to pass SkPicture::serialize a SkSerialProcs with an fTypefaceProc which can properly encode typefaces and then decode with SkPicture::Make with a SkDeserialProcs with an fTypefaceProc which can decode whatever was written. This is how Chromium now handles any non-toy serialization, like with oopr and printing (both of which require sending the serialized picture across process). The default serializer just writes out the font name (if system) or data (if process local) and the default deserializer uses this data to try to recreated the typeface with the default fontmgr.

In theory one way to handle this would be to have the user pass an fontmgr to the picture deserialization part (in the example, as another parameter to K.MakePicture). Then set the deserialization proc to call into a new SkTypeface::MakeDeserialize that takes an SkFontMgr and uses that instead of the default. This is still strictly incorrect as it assumes that this one fontmgr can deserialize any typeface (there may be many fontmgr with different kinds of support) but at least it would allow this obvious case.

subject: Protect FreeType face with mixed glyph formats.
message:
The first in possible a series where I try to figure out how to use the increasingly difficult to use FreeType API.

The next one is how to handle SVG when we don't actually support it. We need to have FT_LOAD_COLOR set on the first load so that we can get color bitmaps, but that flag also prioritizes SVG over outlines (if SVG support is compiled into FreeType). So if the SVG for some reason fails (like we have no SVG hooks, the SVG is invalid, or whatever) we will need to re-load the glyph without FT_LOAD_COLOR (which unfortunately will skip any existing color bitmaps, but I suppose that's fine) and make another pass at it. Which is why I'm interested in the ScalerContextBits, since it will be needed to communicate these awkward situations.

subject: [svg] Add support for `var` in color parsing.
message:
Adding a link [0]. Note that I believe the justification for this is that Chapter 6 of the SVG spec says that `Except for any additional SVG-specific rules explicitly mentioned in this specification, the normative definition of properties that are shared with CSS and XSL is the definition of the property from the CSS2 specification [CSS2].` So browsers generally parse the svg properties with a css parser, which will have support for `var`.


[0] https://drafts.csswg.org/css-variables/#using-variables

[1] https://www.w3.org/TR/SVG11/styling.html

subject: [svg] Add support for `var` in color parsing.
message:
Yes. The spec actually calls this out `If there are any var() references in the fallback, substitute them as well.` [0] Even went and tested this in Chrome to see if it works in general and it does. Though it isn't really nesting in the spec. In the specification `var` expansion happens after tokenization but before the parse (at least logically, the terms used in the spec are somewhat misleading). It can be seen as a "pre-parse parse" which happens at the token level. If the initial --identifier in the `var` exists then the tokens it is defined to have replaces the `var` and any tokens after the `,` in the `var` are discarded. If the --identifier does not exist then the tokens after the `,` in the `var` replace the `var` and the process continues from there. `var` is way more like macro expansion than a function. There are weird side effects because of this, like long form css properties having potentially strange behavior that one would not expect. And yes, this means that if new vars are introduced, removed, or modified a full re-parse is necessary (though not re-tokenization).

In this particular case this is only attempting to support `var` for colors as specified in OT-SVG and SVGNative. So instead of supporting the general case (we don't even do tokenization) I'm just storing off the var identifiers so we can look them up later. It's all a bit squidgy because there is no real specification for this and since this parser doesn't follow the css rules for tokenization anyway I can't really implement the real thing without re-writing everything.


Checking, I see that svg-native-viewer seems to have punted on supporting this with a TODO [1].

[0] https://drafts.csswg.org/css-variables-1/#using-variables

[1] https://github.com/adobe/svg-native-viewer/blob/f5c2ab195c6f3eaa76c2037817fd0d21b505bbc1/svgnative/src/SVGStringParser.cpp#L1097

In the spec this would mean that if `--foo` doesn't exist then the `var` should be replaced by no tokens. Which means that the method would not have recognized any colors if `--foo` wan't defined. I think the equivalent might be a color with type `kNone`?  If this color were encountered (the user doesn't specify this color) then I think the resolver should fail? Maybe? You are correct that we don't want to hard fail here though, because we do want to allow `--foo` a chance. For the time being it may just be better to let it be the default black (I think that's what you get for specifying an color with an empty string).

For example, it would be nice if all the sweep gradients in circles had an extra set of fixed (reference) thin wedges around the circle where the stops should more or less end up. Each wedge having the color of the associated stop. subject: Add optional OT-SVG support to FreeType
message:
Yes, we're going to probably want something like that. Unfortunately, the only way to know the bounds of an SVG glyph is to just render it, which means parsing it, which generally means creating a DOM. However, we would need to know how big the DOM is, we'd need to stick it in the glyph cache somewhere, and we'd also want some way to get the DOMs evicted from the cache before other things. As a first pass I'm fine with not caching anything (even the bounds finding needs a lot of work and is overly slow at the moment).

Note that we'd generally only do this twice for each glyph (per SkScalerContext) since the StrikeCache is going to cache the metrics and then cache the result of any draw calls. In theory we could cache across all the glyphs a given SVG document covers, though that would be an interesting cache. While this single SVG document supporting multiple glyphs is a thing we need to support, it doesn't seem to get used extensively, mostly just for bases+accents and such. Most OT-SVG fonts seem to be constructed such that each glyph has its own small SVG document all to itself. So generally speaking this isn't parsing one enormous SVG which contains all of the glyph drawing for the whole font (though that is in theory possible).

subject: Clone the contents of SkFontArguments when storing the key of the FontCollection typeface cache
message:
Yeah, nothing should ever be holding on to a `SkFontArguments` and this should probably be removed or replaced with `FontArguments`. If you want to hold onto any of the `SkFontArguments` data outside the call that the `SkFontArguments` was passed to a copy of the data should be made (much like `SkFontData` or `SkFontDescriptor` do internally).

The entire point of `SkFontArguments` is to not own anything (all the pointers are borrowed). It is literally an abstraction over passing a bunch of raw pointer parameters and lengths to a method. This abstraction means that more "parameters" can be added later (like the palette was) without needing to update all the functions this data needs to pass through. However, it does mean that one shouldn't hold onto it.

This CL goes most of the way to realizing this, but it should probably go all the way and just create a `FontArguments` (which does own all the data) and immediately drop the idea of having an `SkFontArguments`, potentially just creating an `SkFontArguments` temporary from the `FontArguments` should that ever been needed.

message: This was motivated by the complexity of figuring out when to use COLRv0 or COLRv1 in SkScalerContext_FreeType::generateImage (and with the SVG change, if SVG was actually picked). Currently it is necessary to check for the presence of each format in the same way as was done in generateMetrics. It can be a bit expensive to go poking about in the font data to see if various formats are supported, so we don't want to do it more than we need to. But generateMetrics knows which one it picked, so could just use some of these bits as a private enum to just tell generateImage what to do directly. subject: guard against bad sub run count and size hint
message: It's interesting that this is really a "developer" assert. We do want this assert when we're normally running tests and the like, but we kinda don't want this assert around (or maybe log but not fail) when built for the fuzzer (a debug log developer asserts build?). We need to be able to handle the case correctly, so this assert isn't really asserting a precondition, it's asserting that other code is correct. The fuzzer is "correct" to write garbage into the buffer, but for all other code it is incorrect to write a negative value. In theory this assert should go into all writers of the buffer (except the fuzzer) but that's potentially every write in the process, so can't really do that. Don't know what to do about that, but it's interesting.

message: I am against this setup in general. At the very least all the "trace" stuff must be macros that are only enabled by very specific builders. Second, even if this were completely out of all other builders I do not see how the resulting numbers could possibly be stable or relevant. I don't think this change by itself will detect the issue with the android x86 bot, because that bot will not run its tests just because these files changed (its a terrible setup, but that's how it managed to land in Chromium the first time).

subject: Reland "Reland "Adding a trace to nanobench for RP/VM comparison""
message:
And I claim this does no such thing. If you wanted to even do timing you also need to have compile barriers and fences or the compiler can just move your code around. Even then, without all tests being on the same machine, with the machine running a real time OS or a minimal OS without any task switching or core migration, with all actions deterministically locked to a single thread of execution, etc, etc, I don't see how these tiny measurements are relevant or correct. Even then that won't be entirely interesting since how these differently load threads is also of interest. This will measure more noise than signal. We already consider most of our benches run in nanobench to be misleading at best, and these would be no different.

If we want to time RasterPipeline vs SkVM then just build with each and run, time, and profile real tests like the skp tests. You need real sized tests to get any real numbers. There are too many other interactions happening.

subject: Support for COLR foreground color in CoreText.
message:
CoreText here makes more obvious the issue with how to handle alpha in the glyph fill color. On the other backends we're currently using whatever is on the paint as the fill color, including the alpha. COLR palette entries may have alpha themselves, so it seems fine for the current color to also have alpha. However, the alpha on the paint will also be applied to the whole glyph when it is composited. These are two possibly distinct alphas. We're essentially overriding the paint's color with a shader that looks like a glyph, but that doesn't override the alpha of the paint.

I don't think we need to make everything consistent right now, but will need to think about this.

I don't understand the existence of this enum, nor all the switching. All of these can be better passed in to the constructor directly down in the DEF_GM. Currently the constructor is taking this enum and then this class is expanding that into some set parameter pack. This is very strange organization, just let the caller set the parameters (and the test name, etc).

This is in fact why all the `sets` on SkFontArguments return SkFontArguments&, so that a new one can be created and set up and then passed directly, without needing to name the temporary. Likewise PaletteOverride can be compile time brace initialized, especially when `colorOverrides*` aren't std::vectors but just pointers.

In other words, just pass the `const char* name` and `const SkFontArguments& args` directly to the constructor and set them up in the parameter list of the constructor call in DEF_GM below.

Since the web has a thing about setting palette data, perhaps this means we should suggest that FreeType add a means of setting palette entries much like this (and much like setting axes in a variable font).

message: I think the larger issue here is that none of this is needed at all. The only reason we resolve and cache the axis values is because the FreeType API of FT_Set_Var_Design_Coordinates take the axis values as a FT_Fixed array. There is no way to set them individually, so we do the work of resolving the user request of tags and values to indexes and clamped values and this is quite a bit of work so it is cached. With the palette on the other hand, we can just pass the palette index and any overrides around instead of resolving the whole palette. Then just set up the FT_Face palette directly. This also has the side benefit of pluming the palette index and overrides around so they can be reported later if we want to. Also, we can avoid round trips between FT_Color and SkColor. (Which would be needed if SkFontData stays in SkFontDescriptor.h. While I think it can and should move now, I'd prefer not to do that in this CL.)

message:
I'm not sure I want to try to make this distinction at the typeface level, as this is really a glyph level decision. The real issue is just the decision to force generation from path for the whole scaler context is there is a stroke. This should be pushed to when the metrics and image are generated with SkScalerContext maybe having common code to handle the common case of handling creating metrics or images from the path, but it should be up to the implementing sub-classes of SkScalerContext to decide on a glyph by glyph basis what to do.

Note that with the whole passing in the color bit, that was fine. While it might be wasteful on the cache side to cache lots of the same sort of A8 mask (if the glyphs happened to be A8) that's fine. But I don't want to shut off stroking for any A8 masks just because there happen to be some other tables present in the font file.

subject: [bazel] Try adding cc_binary rules that use generated rules
message:
Interesting. So in our current GN build we have something like

    optional("fontmgr_custom") {
      deps = [ ":typeface_freetype" ]
      public = [ "src/ports/SkFontMgr_custom.h" ]
      sources = [ "src/ports/SkFontMgr_custom.cpp" ]
    }

and the "fontmgr_custom_*" then depend on that. Here we're just depending on SkFontMgr_custom_src directly, which means we also need to bring in the dep on :typeface_freetype. But SkFontMgr_custom_empty_src (and this cc_library) doesn't depend on :typeface_freetype, only SkFontMgr_custom_src does. So this is kinda spreading around the SkFontMgr_custom_src dependencies, which is awkward.

In our current GN build it looks like all the fontmgr_custom_* depend on :typeface_freetype, but they actually don't. Probably should clean that up (not that it was enforced before).

All this to say that in the build, it would probably be better to have a fontmgr_custom target which has public headers and the source and the dep, and then depend on that.

In fact this, kinda goes further than that. The reason why SkFontMgr_custom_empty_src should be able to include SkFontMgr_custom_hdr isn't because SkFontMgr_custom_empty_src happened to #include the header, but because the target SkFontMgr_custom_empty_src is in depends on a fontmgr_custom target which exports SkFontMgr_custom_hdr as a public header. It kinda make the who gazelle thing a bit iffy sounding, since it violates reasoning about dependencies in order to get headers. This seems like gn without check, and no way to add check back?

subject: Fix style parsing with better style.
message: Note this is a pragmatic decision to be cw. Skia is y-down and positive angles are visually clockwise (at least that's how sweep angles seem to be defined). OpenType is y-up and negative angles are visual clockwise. Taking and reporting this consistent with the rest of Skia allows for a direct answer to the question, "If I want to draw an angle to match what do I pass in to Skia?". However, it does mean that this will have the opposite sign of a typical 'ital' variation value since that will be specified in OpenType units. I think this will end up ok, since this is how CSS works (positive angles visually clockwise, but 'ital' axis values will need to be negated from that).

subject: More angle brackets for system includes for third_party deps
message:
Yeah, the difference between <> and "" is interesting. The language specification specification is that <> searches an "implementation-dependent list of places" and "" searches for a file "in an implementation-dependent manner". Which isn't exactly helpful.

Generally, everyone expects "" to be includes from the current project (header files which the current project controls, which the current project could in theory make public as part of its build) and <> is for including things from other projects (which may be built independently and the current project doesn't normally really change or export). Basically, if I own it and could export it if I felt like it "", else <>.

This of course gets muddy with bazel which is based on blaze which grew out of the idea that everything is going to be built into one big statically liked lump and it doesn't matter who owns the code or API or ABI or what not, because nothing is separately compiled or versioned.

message:
C++ is rather frustrating in that proxy iterators have been in the std (vector<bool>) forever but still don't work well so even std::ranges::zip_view doesn't exist yet, even in our future. boost::zip_iterator tried and ran into the same issues. I was going to try to suggest to not make the copy and use something like SkZip and sort that, but it seems even standards groups can't figure it out.

I suppose this is fine for now. I suppose the whole vector of ColorStop is usually no bigger than a vector size_t of indexes.

There are so many language failings here. The swap isn't part of the type of 'sort' (instead depending on ADL). I suppose one could try to abuse ADL to do a 'double swap' but it's rather ugly. The fact that proxy iterators are disallowed from being forward_iterators by a complex interaction of requirements (the reference_type must be a reference to the value_type for forward_iterator).

message:
It seems quite unfortunate the the default for multiple is single and cannot be multiple, so it isn't possible to create a good default. Seems the default for multiple is somewhat useless then, which is unfortunate. So we'll always end up needing a bunch of flags specified like '--included_codec=' is used many times in the invocation of bazel in the canvaskit/Makefile. The issue being that if we use multiple like this we cannot provide a sensible default from which the user can add or subtract, the user always has to specify everything they want explicitly, always. Which is fine I suppose, so long as we end up doing some documentation so that when someone does a default build and gets a Skia library that doesn't do fonts or image decoding and is slow because of no opts that they need to be asking for those things. In GN we never had the option to try out a multiple like thing, so options for optional targets were just given 'namespaced' similar names to relate like things (but each still had its own name, so can be selected or not independently of other things).

All that to explain why I'm not sure excited about multiple. Though if it can be made to work well enough that's fine. It's just weird to run into such a limitation so early.

subject: Ease HarfBuzz API change with feature detection
message:
Thanks, I spent a bunch of time trying to figure out a better way to do this, but an anonymous typedef'ed enum without a specified underlying type seems to be the most difficult thing to detect the existence or non-existence of. Then I realized that the compiler is just going to turn this into an integer anyway.

subject: [infra] Add initial Bazel rules and files
message:
This is fine for now, but note that setting up the fontmgr stuff in a sane way will be interesting (as it is in gn). We really want to allow building in as many fontmgr implementations as possible given the build conditions, but then pick a "_factory.cpp" for exactly one of the ones available, defaulting to the most common if not otherwise stated by the build configuration.

In other words, having a "_factory.cpp" in the select with an implementation on another arm of the select is not what is going to be wanted eventually.

Also keep in mind that we have some tests that are specific to specific fontmgr implementations. We want these to be gathered up into the final set of tests, but only if the associated fontmgr is being built.

In gn we did this with a lot of creating a number of targets which either had things in them or were empty, so that users of those targets could always just depend on them (like targets fontmgr_fontconfig and fontmgr_fontconfig_test which could them be depended on by the skia target or the tests target). Not sure if that makes the most sense here or not.

subject: expose Font to JetSki
message:
What is really wanted is a way for the user to provide a callback thingy which is given the state of shaping after a shaping call and can produce the next 'Font' object to use to shape (and incidentally to font selection also state what ranges should be re-shaped). Unfortunately, the current shaping API is also not great, so not forcing you to write something correct.

Typeface objects should come from a font manager, which will provide some means of matching typefaces, one criteria which may be a family name but may also include style name, the family name in multiple languages, weight, width, slant (these three possibly as ranges), italic, monospace, language, character coverage, color support, axis tag support, feature support, etc.

In general I would have nothing against going from FontManager -> Font, though then one would need to expose a Typeface object to get off of the Font or expose all the interesting bits of SkTypeface on the Font.

That being said, most of the issue I have here is about pretending that one can create a Font from a String (assumed to be a family name). This is pernicious and a common misconception (it's what people think they're doing when they select a font name from a drop down, or what they think they're doing when writing a css font-family list) but it isn't how things work. There is actually a really complicated and policy heavy set of things going on in these cases which requires full font management.

subject: Roll HarfBuzz from 6f190943 to a52c6df3 (2 commits)
message:
A URL starts with `https:' -- which looks like a git trailer if it's in the last 'paragraph' of the commit message and there is nothing not trailer looking before it in the 'paragraph'. So git automatically cleans up this 'badly formatted trailer' and ensures a single space after the ':'. Essentially the same way that such URLs are valid C++ when on their own line, since the part before the ':' is considered a label and the '//' introduces a comment. Even adding '--no-post-rewrite --cleanup=verbatim' doesn't seem to suppress this 'cleanup'. This happens no matter how the commit message was provided, with '-m' or '--file=-'. However, it is possible to modify the trailer separator to something else unlikely to be used, by doing something like 'git -c trailer.separators=~ commit ...'.

This also explains why when the commit hook ran to add the Change-Id trailer a newline wasn't added, because there already was a 'https' trailer.

So annoying when all I want to do is drop some bytes into a thing but, surprise, the system is going to slightly alter those bytes sometimes in a non-obvious not well documented way.

subject: Roll HarfBuzz from 6f190943 to a52c6df3 (2 commits)
message: Turns out that adding 'git -c trailer.separators=~ commit ...' did prevent the url being broken up, but this also means that the hook that adds the Change-Id trailer puts a '~' at the *end* of the trailer for some reason (it still uses ':' anyway). I'm not sure what's going on here, so I'm going to change this to just put a useless trailer at the end of the initial commit message to prevent re-interpretation of the actual message.

message:
This is fine, but I think you can also do 'skvm::UPtr{}' here which will value-initialize (set things to 0) as opposed to default-initialize (things left in indeterminate value). The 'skvm::UPtr{0}' is C for universal zero (it even works for zero sized structs) and 'skvm::UPtr{}' is more or less the C++ equivalent. Note that these two are treated very differently depending on compiling for C or C++.

In any event, this is fine and probably a better idea anyway.

message:
Yeah, function detection won't do anything about the deprecation warning. I initially thought the issue was that CTGetCoreTextVersion was simply not declared if the minimum version was higher, but instead it is declared but marked deprecated.

dlsym isn't that bad, and we've only recently removed many uses when dropping 10.10 support. It's actually not much more expensive than the first time symbol lookup of any other external symbol. We'd probably not want to do it every time though, so should probably initialize once with an SkOnce.

I'd rather start with dlsym anyway, otherwise in the future when CTGetCoreTextVersion is gone we still will need to compile for, say 10.15, but on say 14 it won't exist at all, so better to check for the symbol itself instead of version checking.

It's frustrating to do version checking for version checking, but we're currently using this to work around bugs and otherwise difficult to detect changes in behavior.

That being said, this is fine for now. I can do the dlsym stuff later when needed.

It seems the base debian10 image doesn't have clang and the build script currently really wants to build with clang (CXX=/usr/local/bin/clang++). subject: Experimental ICU runtime linking
message:
So this was already bad and this is more bad piled on top.

First off, this SkUnicode stuff really needs to be a separate module, it shouldn't be in SkShaper at all. The entire point of SkUnicode was to be a separable interface which SkParagraph, SkText, SkShaper, etc could use.

The target name was already wrong, it should be skia_unicode_sources (not skia_shaper_icu_sources, there shouldn't be 'shaper' in this name at all) since the entire point of SkUnicode was to make it's users unaware of the actual implementation (which could be ICU but could be something else). So putting this SkICU.h in here with SkUnicode is really bad since it's totally defeating the point of the existence of SkUnicode.

Where this becomes really bad though is that it becomes possible to incorrectly define "SK_RUNTIME_ICU_XXX" in the skshaper component, which should be impossible. The skshaper component should not only be unaware of this, it shouldn't even be able to affect the build of SkICU at all.

subject: Experimental ICU runtime linking
message:
Actually, now that I've thought about it for a while, this SkICU thing should probably be part of the SkUnicode module (just that the SkUnicode module needs to be moved out of SkShaper module). The idea is that SkUnicode_icu.cpp should be the only thing that actually uses ICU (that's the point, to hide the implementation) so this new SkICU thing really belongs with it, though it might want to be named SkUnicode_icu.h, SkUnicode_icu_builtin.cpp, and SkUnicode_icu_runtime.cpp.

The issue I had in particular was that SkShaper was configuring the content of the SkUnicode build though setting the build macros and such. SkShaper shouldn't be doing that as it should simply be depending on and using SkUnicode.

subject: [canvaskit] Add Typeface.MakeFreeTypeFaceFromData
message:
The Skia side SkTypeface::MakeFrom* are a real pain since they rely on a magic singleton global in a library. If we were writing Skia from scratch we wouldn't want SkFontMgr::RefDefault to exist, and at this point it mostly only exists for our tests, which is not a good reason. The user should always create the appropriate factory (or factories) and use it. Since we have to opportunity to avoid such an API mistake here, I'm against adding it. No other library has a weird thing like this, DirectWrite and CoreText create only IDWriteFont and CTFont, respectively. Cairo has specific function calls to create FreeType, LOGFONT, CGFont, User, or Toy fonts explicitly, with no generic create from data. QT has QRawFont which uses whatever QFontDatabase is using and seems to explicitly only allow one backend (selected at compile time, also QT is way higher level and far more opinionated).

Basically, either guarantee that there will every only be exactly one factory ever (only FreeType) and remove all of the FontMgr.MakeTypeface* and use only SkTypeface::MakeFrom*, or don't make this guarantee and have only FontMgr.MakeTypeface* and no SkTypeface::MakeFrom*. Either way, anything which can be done not to use SkFontMgr::RefDefault ever is a good idea.

That being said, avoiding SkFontMgr::RefDefault is still a pain since SkFontMgr still hasn't been split into SkFontFactory and the SkFontCollection.

subject: SkTypeface_FreeType to own FT_Face
message:
So previously an FT_Face existed for an SkTypeface_FreeType if any SkScalerContext_FreeType existed (was in the cache). With this change an FT_Face will exist on any SkTypeface_FreeType which has been "used" in any way. The following sizes are from a 64bit build, and there are a lot of pointers, so these are smaller on a 32bit build. This also removes 16 bytes per existing FT_Face and a linked-list search on each call into SkTypeface_FreeType or SkScalerContext_FreeType.

An FT_FaceRec is itself 248 bytes, plus space for a cached family name, style name, list of available bitmap sizes (32 bytes each), metadata on each character map (16 bytes each), another 128 bytes for internal data (FT_Face_InternalRec_), plus autohinting data if it's been created, which is generally a set of six or so blue zones.

The actual TT_FaceRec one gets from creating an sfnt font is 1472 bytes (including an embedded FT_FaceRec), plus the current palette data. This TT_FaceRec size includes a number of local cached copies of frequently used fixed sized tables (and fixed size headers to tables) like the header, hhea, maxp, vhea, name, OS/2, post (no glyph names), gasp. Note that if the FT_Stream is memory based the cmap table data is referred to directly, if not an in-memory copy of the currently selected cmap will be made. Similarly the font and cvt programs along with the original cvt table values, the hdmx, sbit, and kern tables will be used directly if the FT_Stream is memory based but copies may be made to bring them into memory if needed. Strings from the name table are only actually loaded when requested, but once loaded don't unload.

So, generally speaking, I would expect extra use of ~2KB per SkTypeface_FreeType which is "used" but has no SkScalerContext_FreeType entries in the strike cache. This seems to line up with actual measurement. Given this, the actual question is why not always create the FT_Face on SkTypeface_FreeType creation like we do on macOS and DirectWrite? This small step to wait until "use" was done to ensure that it's still possible to create a large number of SkTypeface_FreeType and only pay for the FT_Face that are actually needed, since the FreeType backend tends to be used more often in resource constrained environments. I believe the whole caching of FT_Face was done on Android originally to avoid forcing the FT_Faces into every process even if it didn't need them (though now Android just mmaps every font file in the system anyway).

In a very constrained environment, I don't see this change making a big difference. It seems likely that there won't be that many font files available to begin with, so once used they're likely to have an SkScalerContext in the strike cache anyway, which would have keep the FT_Face active.

subject: check for bad int-bounds passed to canvas.
message:
I'm somewhat concerned about this because what you're actually trying to do here is clean up after having performed an undefined operation. Casting a float to an int where the float value is out of range of the int is undefined behavior, so sufficiently advanced compilers may end up doing strange things to this (if the compiler knows that the caller always uses a large but positive value, isEmpty can be inferred never to return true, so you could get a negative value anyway). It just so happens that on Intel cvttsd2si and related instructions map out of range conversions of this sort to INT_MIN. So as long as the compiler doesn't propagate the undefined part of the behavior down here that's what you'll get on Intel. No idea on Arm.

Either the calling code should sanitize the values, or the direct cast should be replaced with something safe like http://stackoverflow.com/questions/25857843/how-do-i-convert-an-arbitrary-double-to-an-integer-while-avoiding-undefined-beha#answer-26584177 . I don't really see the point of adding the asserts if we're relying on undefined behavior for them to work.

subject: Change makeArrayDefault into makeArray or makeUninitializedArray

subject: [COLRv1] Paint cycle detection
message:
In some distant future the standard library may eventually get real hash tables like flat_map and flat_set (and hopefully stop using generic sounding names for specific implementations). In any event, unordered_set is kinda bad, especially for this sort of constant pushing and popping. Can we use SkTHashSet here?

There are examples of how to use it and create the required hash function for SkTHashSet at tests/HashTest.cpp, in particular the part with CopyCounter. A more real example might be OneLineShaper::FontKey::Hasher::operator() in OneLineShaper.cpp.

subject: [COLRv1] Paint cycle detection
message:
Sure, std::unordered_* is basically required to be chained and not open (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hash_table#Collision_resolution ). SkTHashTable and related continues to exist because flat_map/flat_set (open addressed) haven't made it into the standard yet.

The biggest issue with chained is that it more or less requires new/delete for each insert or remove (there are implementations that try to work around this with lots of overhead though). When just adding everything once and then doing lots of reads open is still better, but it is something of a wash overall since cpus are good at pointer chasing. However, when adding and removing a lot but not dramatically changing the size often (like here) open tends to win by a lot (if not marking slots dead) since there is so much less memory management.

Note that some open addressing implementations can run into issues with load factors when removing elements if it just marks slots dead, but SkTHashTable::removeSlot does the optimization of moving later colliders on removal. This means that one doesn't run into the delete load factor issues.

subject: GN: Use //gn:warnings only for Skia targets.
message:
This seems quite awkward. What is really being said is that if there are multiple projects in a build using gn then one really should be avoiding build globals in general (use of set_defaults). It seems gn itself does not really support a project scope (set_defaults for only a glob or namespace of targets). This is true all the way down to the toolchains (set_default_toolchain), where in theory each target (all the way down to the file level) could explicitly state its toolchain (and not implicitly through set_default_toolchain and having files with a particular extension). Or the toolchains could be explicitly placed into some namespace so they could be explicitly implied (much like if set_default_toolchain could take a target glob or target glob or prefix or something). Really what is wanted it to build all of Skia's third_party stuff in it's own build system (even if that build system happens to be Skia maintained BUILD.gn files) and then link Skia against those (the same way Skia would link against system libraries). Currently Dawn is built inside Skia's build directly so gets all the set_defaults and set_default_toolchain, but it seems the only thing really desired to be shared here is the toolchain definition so the build works on the bots? Of course, if the Dawn build depends on certain things being in set_defaults (does it? like NDEBUG and whatnot?) then they would also need to be set though set_defaults, with the reverse issue of Skia targets now getting additional config (potentially).

Essentially the idea here is to use the skia_private config as a kind of project namespace instead of using default_configs through set_defaults. The awkward part is that it feels like Skia is being squeezed out of its own build system. The alternative way to look at it is that pulling as much out of BUILDCONFIG.gn and set_defaults and putting it into configs makes the Skia build more flexible and explicit. I'll go on a walk and think about it.

subject: GN: Use //gn:warnings only for Skia targets.
message: With https://skia-review.googlesource.com/c/skia/+/385516 now landed and sticking, the goal of this CL should now be met. The //gn/skia:warnings are only applied to skia_* targets (and only in the Skia build), leaving the base target types like executable, source_set, shared_library, static_library, and component more generic. If there are any further issues where the base target types should be even more generic, let us know. Now that all the framework is in place it should be simple to shuffle configs around.

subject: GN: Use //gn:warnings only for Skia targets.
message: There is one wrinkle that may be of interest, which is that //gn/skia:warnings adds lots of warnings but also removed a number of warnings (lots of -Wno-*). As a result it is possible to run into the case where Skia targets may have warnings enabled which weren't enabled before (in particular unused-parameter can be one of these). We may end up changing things so that the '-Wno-*' are always applied to make it easier for other projects to crank up their own warnings without needing to do anything special for the Skia targets. If it turns out you need this, let us know.

message: I think NonBreakingSpace is a bit too specific. This is more like 'BetterThanGraphemeLineBreakBefore'. It may make more sense to use a few bits as a 'LineBreakPriority' number since there's really a list of places to look for making line breaks. These are something like 'must break', 'normal break location', 'hyphenation break location' (though this one isn't used here), 'split word break location' (this one, since it's something like a hyphenation break), 'grapheme break location', and 'glyph break location' (try to never break on one of these). In general one tries to break from highest to lowest priority on these and I'm not sure it makes sense to even keep track of a lower priority one over a higher priority one for a given code unit.

10 white-space break BREAK_WHITESPACE
15 word break BREAK_WORD
20 intraword break BREAK_INTRA
30 letter break BREAK_LETTER
40 clip break BREAK_CLIP

These are to be considered from lowest value (highest priority) to highest value (lowest priority). This new one is something like BREAK_INTRA.

subject: allocation system for properly aligned bytes
message:
It seems the generic minimum size is '(kMaxAlignment - 1) + sizeof(Block) + requestedSize' since (working from the end of the block) this will need to align Block to kMaxAlignment, wasting up to 'kMaxAlignment - 1' bytes to do so, then have requestedSize bytes left over at the beginning of the block. This could also be written as 'requestedSize + sizeof(Block) + (kMaxAlignment - 1)' to be in low-to-high memory order, but it's a little less descriptive that way.

For the char* passed in from the constructor the pointer and size are passed directly, so no need for slop (no need to calculate the minimum size, could just check where things will end up since the alignment of the end is known). The Storage type knows requestedSize but not what the beginning or end will be (which may be of any alignment) so needs this full pessimistic calculation. For internal use when calling 'new' the base is alignof(max_align_t) which may be smaller than kMaxAlignment which is what this method currently tries to handle.

subject: allocation system for properly aligned bytes
message:
Maybe name this maxTrailingBytes or something?

We know alignof(Block) <= maxAlignment. The idea is that the memory can be thought of as being in chunks of size assumedAlignment (because the code below aligns size up to a multiple of assumedAlignment).

When assumedAlignment <= maxAlignment a Block can be placed once every (maxAlignment / assumedAlignment) chunks . This means that at most (maxAlignment / assumedAlignment) - 1 chunks could go unused. Going from units of chunks to bytes means multiplying by assumedAlignment (the size of a chunk in bytes) which gives (maxAlignment - assumedAlignment).

When maxAlignment < assumedAlignment it is only necessary to align up to maxAlignment since the base will already be over aligned. There doesn't seem much use in this over aligning since it can't be made to work (the over alignment is lost after basing calculation off the Block position which won't be as aligned). It is interesting that this calculation handles the over alignment case but the minimum size calculation does not.

subject: Add support for retina displays to sk_app.
message:
The idea is for the units on the Skia side to be in terms of raw pixel size, then have the scale (in Viewer the fZoomFactor) default to the window scale factor so the drawing would be scaled up to size. In this case since svg and skottie are tracking the window size (now reported in raw pixels) and the default fZoomFactor is a scale by two, they are drawn 4x as big as they used to be (when we wanted just 2x). (Before the window size was in 'big pixels" and the fZoomFactor default was identity.)

The issue here being that the gms are generally written in terms of "big pixel" units which we want to scale up on a retina device so that they end up more or less the same physical size on the screen and not tiny. The svg and skottie views which resize to the window size are in window units which used to be "big pixel" units and are now "raw pixel" units. So the real issue here is that different base zooms are wanted. We could split this out in Viewer from the fZoomFactor (fBackingFactor) and have the slide tell us if it is hi-dpi aware and does not need the fBackingFactor (it is already hi-dpi aware by virtue of using the window bounds to scale itself). Note there are two different ways to use the window bounds, one to do scale / stretch and one to simply draw more and a greater density.

Splitting out the backing scale factor is probably a good idea anyway, since fZoomFactor is applied exponentially so it's rather difficult to get back to 1:1 from 2:1 scale using it.

message:
I wrote up a change to avoid all the string copies and... it didn't make a difference to the time. I looks like with our svgs (the pubic ones pulled by infra/bots/assets/svg/create.py) that bumping the buffer size to 4096 brings down the debug runtime to basically the release runtime.

Running "perf record out/asan/dm --config svg --src svg --svgs out/svg" before and after this change shows that the entire difference is in "normal_scanLt()", where in the debug case (with the small buffer) it spends 26% of the total time of the running program. In any event, I'm convinced this is the case, and this code in particular isn't very subject to slicing since it's more or less written once and hands off the full accumulated text to subclasses.

subject: Bump SkXMLParser buffer size
message:
This seems to be a copy-paste from SkFontMgr_android_parser.cpp#parse_config_file, except it lacks the comment stating why this was done, which is to detect when XML_CharacterDataHandlers aren't appending (it's easy to write them in such a way that they don't realize that they may be called multiple times for a single run of character data if it spills over the edge of a single buffer).

In this case this class itself never handles the character data itself, the ctx->appendText does, but then those need to be sure to be written correctly as well. In any event, if that doesn't matter this change is fine.

On the other hand if everything was really as slow as stated, the issue is probably that the ctx->appendText was inefficiently using SkString and appending to it, resulting in n^2 concatenation time. If that is the case using a string builder of some sort and snapping off strings would be far more efficient.

subject: Bump SkXMLParser buffer size
message: This is probably the real issue, that this is an SkString. This should be more like a std::vector<char> or something so that it doesn't grow every time an append happens and doesn't free the entire backing store every time flushText is called.

subject: Bump SkXMLParser buffer size
message:
This is either a great size or a terrible size. If the malloc in XML_GetBuffer keeps all data about this block out of line then this will end up on many systems nicely being one 4KB page. On the other hand if it doesn't this can actually allocate two full pages and mostly waste one of them. I wish there were some c library call for "I want some memory at least this size, but no bigger than some other size, please go efficiently do that and tell me how much you gave me". We want something like that for the arena allocator and the dynamic memory stream implementation and like all over the place.

In other words, I wish I could say something about this number other than that I'm slightly depressed about it. I'm fine with this number being larger (especially in release) but I can't really tell you the right number. Only the allocator knows, and it isn't telling.

subject: Make sure maxIntrinsicWidth is always no less than minIntrinsicWidth
message:
These values are actually the width of everything laid out on one line (calling that 'max') and the maximum width of everything laid out on as many lines as natural (calling that 'min'). But these are just different measurements. Currently what's allowing this to mostly work is the idea of chopping up a single line into bits, but in the general case nothing at all is making one of these measurements bigger or smaller than the other (not just rounding). It's actually unfortunate that these measurements are thought of as 'min' and 'max' since they're actually just unrelated measurements that happen to often be ordered that way.

In any event, I suppose its fine to always yank the max up to the min.

subject: Fix up a ton of implicit memory_order_seq_cst for unique id gen
message:
After staring at the code for a while I don't see anywhere where the value of the id implies anything about any other bit of memory or that some other bit of memory if accessible. For example, we don't ever seem to assume that because id N is available that some object is accessible (the only map from id to object is the cache and that already needed to be thread safe) or some other object is accessible (the existence of id N doesn't give us access to id N-1).

So I say ship it, since if there are any issues which are going to result from this I'm not going to find them by inspection.

subject: Fix up a ton of implicit memory_order_seq_cst for unique id gen
message:
Oddly, it seems we increment these ids so often and therefore execute so many barriers to TSAN (it also emits actual barriers like MFENCE which is the perf warning, but I'm more interested in the TSAN bits here) that I can imagine these fences potentially covering other possible races. Looking through here I don't see anywhere the returned value indicates that anything can be inferred (in most cases we create the id before the object is created, so the existence of an id doesn't even imply the existence of an object). As a result, I'm actually more concerned about this uncovering different latent bugs elsewhere than this change breaking any of the code which deals with ids.

In any event, I kicked off some TSAN bots just to look.

subject: Fix GCC optimization issue by laundering each element of fStorage.
message:
So I'm going to be pedantic here, but that's the only way to be with std::launder. This is still undefined behavior (it works in gcc because gcc seems to be using launder as a full break in pointer analysis for that pointer, since things might be insane, like at the bottom of https://miyuki.github.io/2016/10/21/std-launder.html ). The need for std::launder is *after* the 'new'. It seems that just about anywhere the return value of 'placement new T' is disregarded is eventually going to want a std::launder. (Note that it is the pointer returned from launder which is 'laundered', the original pointer is not). I believe if we kept an array of the pointers which came out of these 'placement new T' (including all the others in this file) and used those instead of going through fItemArray offsets (which the compiler is seeing through the aliasing and doesn't think is 'really' a T*) then things would work. Of course, no one is going to do that.

I think generally the only real right way to do it is to make fItemArray just be a 'char*' and std::launder every cast to T*.

Note that the existing code on the left of this particular diff carefully stays in 'char*' and avoids the 'static_cast<T*>(dst_v) + i' since it is really difficult to tell if doing pointer arithmetic in T space is actually legal here (in the end 'new' is just taking it as 'void*' so it might be ok?). I'm almost convinced that going with 'static_cast<T*>(dst_v) + i' won't cause trouble at some point, but I'm not sure enough to bet on it either way.

subject: Fix GCC optimization issue by laundering each element of fStorage.
message:
> I'm also not really sure why we have SkAlignedSTStorage when we can just do `alignas(T) char buf[sizeof(T) * K]`-type setups.

We should (I think) at least try to move to std::aligned_storage, which is used elsewhere. I'm pretty sure that's more or less a direct replacement? Of course, that's pretty much a vocabulary type for exactly what you propose.

subject: Fix GCC optimization issue by laundering each element of fStorage.
message: Also wanted to say that it seems std::launder is insane in that while it is called 'Pointer optimization barrier' in the specification, it requires that an actual object X be present at the location pointed to, so it cannot be used to obtain a X* of a zero sized container (which is at least one reason why patch set 1 doesn't fulfill the requirements). It's more of a 'Pointer to complete object optimization barrier'. (It's kinda like the reason for 'meow::data()' since '&meow::[0]' fails on empty containers.) Now, in theory this shouldn't make a difference since you couldn't access anything through an X* of a zero sized container, but on the other hand calling std::launder on such a thing is technically UB! So I think SkTArray::data would need to be careful not to call 'std::launder(fItemArray)' when empty, since that would technically be undefined behavior.

subject: Cannot create SkFontData with no data.
message:
I've been looking to see why this wasn't already caught. This would have happened decoding any pre-79 version skp with a variable font in it which didn't also store the data. I suppose our skps these days usually have the data embedded. Also the set of system fonts when they are recorded probably doesn't have variable fonts. (Of course with this change the crash is mitigated, but system fonts variable fonts aren't deserialized correctly when the data isn't embedded, since the variation isn't being passed along to the created typeface, though I'm not sure what difference it makes since doing a lookup by name is basically a wild guess that can return anything). It seems we don't have such an skp about, but the fuzzer managed to create one.

The code path in question isn't actually reachable from any current serialization, it's there to pick up and handle old serializations. I don't expect this bit of code to ever really change except to be removed when support is removed for version 79 and earlier skps. The fuzzer created an issue with this bit pattern as an skp, so will keep testing it. I'm not really sure I can make a more interesting test than that. I'll have to think about it.

Interestingly, part of the difficulty with writing such a test in an understandable way it that it means setting up a lot of internal state in the class. If there were an easy way to write a 'this is an in-class test of just the internals of this class' which could be inline in the TU and a friend of the class that would make things easier. The alternative is to write a test which is literally a bunch of hex bytes to deserialize and then make a call and say 'it shouldn't crash'. This seems quite fragile and difficult to explain what the test is doing, and the fuzzer case is already doing that.

subject: [skottie] Auto-resize and VAlign support for point text
message: Do you do this yourself somewhere? Note that SkShaper doesn't handle markup (like considering \n or \r or some combination to be forced line breaks, or \t to be a logical break in the text which needs layout). If you pass it text with \r or\n or such it will probably have a soft line break attached to it (since it's allowable to break between control codepoints and basically anything) but it won't hard line break since that's actually something different. At SkShaper's level there's no difference in how to handle '\t', '\r', ' ', or 'a' except Unicode code point properties. Some fonts do have glyphs for control codepoints like '\r', if so they may be shown. Text passed to SkShaper should already be broken up into "paragraphs" where that means any text which should be shaped together and isn't broken up by breaking markup (like '\t' and '\r' if they are to mean 'tab stop' or 'hard line break'). Otherwise such codepoints will be treated like any other codepoints.

subject: Fix gms placing text in bounds.
message: It was because one way computed the bounds with RGB pixel geometry and another with unknown pixel geometry producing different bounds. Since this used to incorrectly draw the text at the left edge of the bounds (instead of the origin of the bounds) this shifted the glyphs. In theory this should not happen as the pixel geometry of the surface should not affect the glyph metrics, but some code paths do not yet support kGenA8FromLCD. See also https://skia-review.googlesource.com/c/skia/+/319696 (FreeType may also need to be updated).

subject: Fix gms placing text in bounds.
message:
This turns out to be wrong because I misunderstood what this was doing (because the comment is even more misleading than I thought). safeRect is the set of x,y offsets for the string's bounding box (note that it's even used to pass into 'fClipRects[i].offset'. So this adjustment is incorrect since the text needs to be offset the same amount (this was always drawing the text centered in the bounding box).

The oddness of this comes more form lcd vs non-lcd bounds. If we're doing subpixel rendering we will often need a bit more space so the width of the bounds will grow by 2 pixels (1 pixel in each direction). This means that the safeRect will have a different width and so the location chosen for the bounding box will change (since nextRangeScaler will scale a 0..1 value to the range). Note that this also will affect the vertical placement, but we don't normally see it due to baseline snapping. This is different from the lcdoverlap in that this isn't trying to center the text in a bounding box. Instead the oddness of this one comes from the SkFont setting causing the bounding box to change, affecting where the code here places the text.

All that to say, I'm going to fix the comment and the member name to make this clear.

subject: Simplify creation of SkSurfaceProps
message:
So currently (most of) the SkSurface constructors take SkSurfaceProps* so that one can pass in nullptr to mean 'use the globals', which arguably wasn't needed, it could have taken a SkSurfaceProps& and required the user to call SkSurfaceProps(kLegacyFontHost_InitType) to create a temporary to pass in (since that's what is happening when passing nullptr anyway).

If we remove the Skia globals then either the SkSurface constructors continue to take SkSurfaceProps* and nullptr means 'Default' (no flags unknown/flat pixel geometry) instead, or the SkSurface constructors would be migrated to take SkSurfaceProps& and one could pass 'SkSurfaceProps()'. I suppose what I'm getting at here is that we only need this 'Default' thing because we want a pointer and not a reference (and want to avoid as_lvalue or forcing a name to make an lvalue just so we can take the address of the thing).

In any even I think it's probably nicer to just have this return 'const SkSurfaceProps&' and let the callers take the address of it. Even though that's an extra bit at each use site, it points out that the SkSurface constructors are a little weird.

Also, it would be really nice if this were all constexpr.

subject: Simplify creation of SkSurfaceProps
message:
Yet another option is to remove all use from Skia and put the globals and the old behavior behind a flag (which would be set in Chromium's build of Skia to keep the old behavior) and then make the Chromium side change while removing the build flag to both remove the globals and change the behavior of 'nullptr' at the same time (to be kUnknown instead of Legacy).

I've started in on https://skia-review.googlesource.com/c/skia/+/319343 which is more or less what needs to be done Skia side. This has unfortunately uncovered some knock on things which will need to be fixed as well (like https://skia-review.googlesource.com/c/skia/+/319696 and possibly others) where there was a subtle dependency on the globals providing a consistent default.

subject: ICU project: text break iterators in SkShaper
message:
This is a bit frightening. If we have a generic type it should actually be generic.

There are two ways to go about this. The first is to make SkText something which one could wrap in a UText. This is difficult. The second option is to not share the UText (just create two UTexts backed by the same char*).

In this second case we don't need SkText yet (though we should probably have something like it in the future which can wrap non-contiguous text input). Just have setText here create a new UText (it doesn't even need to be new'ed, it could be embedded here in the type and initialized here). The UText doesn't take ownership of or make a copy of the data, so there isn't really much overhead (and less than calling 'new' a bunch).

subject: implement SkUNREACHABLE with SK_ABORT
message: On specifically the subject of "Is the compiler allowed to assume all functions not marked noreturn will always return?" I think https://stefansf.de/post/non-termination-considered-harmful/ does a good job of explaining a lot of the interesting bits. In general a C++ compiler is allowed to assume that forward progress will be made unless certain explicit constructs are used (not just that functions will return, which is included in that). Until C++11 I think the only valid infinite loop was one that relied on a volatile read (I think constants are now allowed as well).

subject: SkUNREACHABLE should fail, not be UB.
message:
So SK_ABORT works, but this is confusing because this is already

    __MACHINE(__declspec(noreturn) void __fastfail(unsigned int))

which lines up with the warning documentation [0]. If I change sk_abort_no_print to __declspec(noreturn) SK_ABORT still works fine. However, if I put sk_abort_no_print in an 'extern "C"' block (like all the intrinsics are declared) then SK_ABORT doesn't work. Presumably putting things in an 'extern "C"' block loses the 'noreturn' bit in msvc. Or at least some part of it, since it seems to satisfy the 'if used in a method it meets the noreturn requirement' (the new sk_abort_no_print is compiling fine) but it doesn't seem to be in a place where the warning looks when it does control flow anaysis.


[0]. https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/error-messages/compiler-warnings/compiler-warning-level-1-c4715?view=vs-2019

subject: SkPathView for ownerless (can live on stack) SkPaths
message:
Just on a high level theoretical basis for why this CL exists and is so big (trying to convince myself). So if we didn't have any existing names to deal with...

This new SkSPath would be named something more like SkPath, it's just a generic base class (really and interface of sorts) with read-only data that describes a path and doesn't itself care about the storage of the path data. It would have a virtual destructor (maybe?).

On top of that would be SkPathPoly<N> (some number of lines passed in and would subsume the 'triangle' and 'quad' classes here), SkPathQuads<N>, maybe something fancier at the limits of inline storage, and a SkPathBuilder which would be used to create paths backed by dynamic storage and would return a subclass of the new SkPath (here called SkSPath) which is basically the SkPath we currently know which is more or less an sk_sp<SkPathRef> except in this hypothetical world SkPathRef isn't editable.

So this CL is basically trying to replace all mention of the current SkPath with SkSPath since it's really the new path interface, but since the current SkPath is editable still we can't really make it a subclass and also there's the desire to try to avoid the virtual destructor, so this 'peek' mechanism which is awkward because it's kind of a stand in for the lack of that virtual destructor on the other end of use (it essentially creates a snap-off of the current SkPath/SkPathRef which is a subclass since the SkPath can't really itself be a subclass). (The 'Triangle' and 'Quad' subclasses are trying to get away with the lack of virtual destructor by avoiding needing a non-trivial destructor and by trying to keep themselves stack only (which they should probably try harder at).

I was thinking about this mostly because the whole 'peek' bit is rather awkward. It seems what we really want is for the current SkPath 'to be a' SkSPath, but instead 'peek' is more of an explicit version of SkPath 'is convertable to' SkSPath. Maybe all of this is just a comment that 'peek' should be called 'asSkSPath' or something like that.

In a range based for loop it's the `auto && __range = range_expression ;` outside the for loop which is keeping the initializer list alive (it's doing lifetime extension).

subject: Make SkRefCnt::getRefCnt public in debug mode
message:
We don't even expose this to ourselves at the moment, only to SkRefCnt internally and only in debug. And even then it's super subtle and I feel iffy about it's use internally. In fact there are subtle issues with this method and unique and SkWeakRefCnt which we should try to fix internally.

I think the bar for debugging use of this method should be making a local code change like this; I don't think it should be upstreamed. Upstreaming would 'normalize' and make it possible a user will check in code which calls this method because it's in base Skia and the CI may not catch it because its available there too. In other words, I think the current situation is working as intended.

It's a crazy footgun. The standard added std::shared_ptr::use_count (and even allowed in non-debug!) for some reason, but I think that's mostly around people being unwilling / unable to touch their own STL to get at it (which should be the bar, the std should at least add a big scary macro you need to define to get it, use outside a paused debugger is always a bug). The bar for local modifications to Skia headers is much lower.

I might be willing to entertain the idea if Skia had a SK_MT_NONE build setting where Skia is built with no thread support at all (all mutexes do nothing / assert not held, any required 'threading' is all done on one thread, the thread safe refcnts are not thread safe, etc). This would require the caller to also not use any threads, which may pose an issue.

subject: Notify when SkFontMetrics bounds are bogus.
Notify when SkFontMetrics bounds are bogus.
message:
I'm not sure we even really want the SkRect* bounds to pass into hasBounds. I did that to follow the style of the other 'hasXXX' methods on SkFontMgr which return a bool and also set a SkScalar to the value if returning true (even though the value set is something the user already has in their hand).

Note that this method (SkTypeface::onComputeBounds) takes in an 'SkRect* bounds' and if this were just returning the bounds directly, just passing through 'bounds' would be fine. However, because of the inflation it's actually less mucking about to just use the 'fm' which has all the values on the stack. It's interesting to see what gcc and clang do with this version and the version where we pass bounds through and multiply it out in-place. With this code here they both do ok, with the version where bounds is passed through gcc sees that everything lines up so does one wide multiply (after much mucking about to get that set up) but clang doesn't seem to optimize any of it and does much worse (using a bunch of mulss instead of one mulps). Seems like clang has difficulty with optimizing the instructions past the conditionals?

After all this mucking about I'm just going to make hasBounds not take an out param since it doesn't seem to actually help anyone (and can hurt). Can add it later if it is wanted I suppose.

message:
Yeah I really want to say
    SkASSERT(!dstArray implies numGlyphs == 0)
which (since we don't have an 'imp' operator) turns into
    SkASSERT(dstArray || numGlyphs == 0)
it also has the nice property of logically short circuiting, though that's a bit silly here.

Since it seems 'imp' is A?B:true this could be written
    SkASSERT(!dstArray ? numGlyphs == 0 : true);
Which leads me to believe that in C++ the implies operator should be written `a??b` which is a binary operator which works like `a?b:true`. The objection would be that the ?? logical operator could have no ? binary operator, but whatever.

But that extra hanging true to make it work is ugly, could be
    constexpr bool implies(bool a, bool b) { return a ? b : true; }
    SkASSERT(implies(!dstArray, numGlyphs == 0));
Though without the infix of implies that looks a bit awkward. 

Of course, since it's the hanging `else true` that's ugly we end up with
    if (!dstArray) { SkASSERT(numGlyphs == 0); }

subject: Cleanup for TextLine::getGlyphPositionAtCoordinate.
message:
I like auto when doing template stuff, and I like it when I only had to name something because I need an intermediate sub result (like I didn't really even want to give the intermediate a name at all, but do to expression complexity or other reasons had to split things up).

Here in particular I was trying to make it obvious what was an x coordinate (SkScalar), what was a UTF-8 offset (TextIndex), and what is some other kind of offset (int/size_t). I would love a language that made it easier to make opaque numeric types with the right operators based on category. Basically, a unit system to prevent adding unlike things (like utf16 and utf8 offsets or even trying to add a vertical offset to a horizontal offset without first coercing them to vectors). If we had things set up with strong opaque types that enforced units, the strong type system could prevent us from mixing things up. In that case I'd be fine with auto. However, in this case we don't really have a strong type system, we're just doing math on a bunch if floats and ints without much regard to the units (and no enforcement from the type system).

Indeed, here I'm more changing the names to show the actual types (apps hungarian) so that it's easier to see where things are going strange. All the 'Pos' and 'Utf8Index' and the like would be much better off in a numeric type that enforced the units.
