subject: Convert SkString::resize to SkString::resetToSize.
message: I don't see the point in removing this, it's a good point.

subject: Convert SkString::resize to SkString::resetToSize.
message: I don't see where we're forcing the length of the SkString back to zero? You're overwriting part of the existing bytes without updating the string length, which seems bad. Note that SkString isn't actually '\0' terminated, it just keeps the extra '\0' around for easy conversion to c string, the SkString is a pointer and length (as all UTF-8 must be, codepoint zero is a perfectly cromulent codepoint and must be handled as one and not as a terminator).

subject: Convert SkString::resize to SkString::resetToSize.
message: Well, no, fLength tracks the actual length of the string, the code assumes that the buffer is of size at least fLength aligned to the next four bytes. fLength must always be the actual length of the string and the data from fBeginningOfData to fBeginningOfData + fLength shouldn't be mucked with unless the user wants it mucked with. Any violation of this is currently a bug.

subject: Convert SkString::resize to SkString::resetToSize.
message:
I suppose what I'm pointing out is that previous callers mostly knew that they were only shortening the string some (usually small, often zero) amount (and logically already had) so they were effectively just modifying fLength without actually doing anything about the existing allocation. More than anything else they were desperately trying to avoid doing allocations or copies just to make the string some tiny amount shorter (often not even changing the length at all).

The issue I have with this change in particular is that it's doing more work but 'resetToSize' is still supposed to produce garbage. If it is supposed to produce garbage then there is no need to do this. If it isn't supposed to produce garbage then it's wrong.

subject: Convert SkString::resize to SkString::resetToSize.
message: This goes against the entire point of the original, which was to avoid as much work as possible, especially in the common case. This code basically enforces the super slow path every time.

subject: Optimize findLimitingClusters
message:
Just to be clear, this maps code unit offsets in fText to a glyph cluster index (and the glyph cluster index is an index into fClusters, not the code unit offset into fText where the current glyph cluster starts which would be 'fClusters[fClusterIndexes[<index into fText>]].fTextRange.start' ).

So this is fClustersIndexFromCodeUnit. It's a way to get from an index in fText to an index in fClusters (can be used for other things as well, but that's what it does). Before you were calculating these values on the fly as needed, and here you're just caching them.

subject: Close file before writing in SkVMTest.
message:
Not sure I understand, everything seems to be doing its job as advertised, the SkData is backed by the file after all. Windows doesn't have *nix file descriptors (though it will fake 'fd' numbers in the c library) it has file HANDLES which are rather different. Here we have an SkData backed by a Windows file HANDLE (in this case in sk_fdmmap). It isn't backed by a FILE* (we closed that), but it is backed by a HANDLE from CreateFileMapping and MapViewOfFile FILE_MAP_READ. Windows really likes locking files and if you call CreateFileMapping it will not allow anything to change the content of the file (except though that CreateFileMapping if opened for write). In addition Windows will not unlink a file HANDLE while it is open (at least not without a serious amount of work afaict), so when you go to open the path for write it will attempt to truncate the file at that path (it will not unlink the existing file at that path and put a new file in its place). Somewhat unrelated Windows also won't let you unlink any file opened for execute, which is one of the reasons Windows updates generally like to reboot and run before anything else starts up.

Note that without closing 'expected' early like this on *nix you end up with 'expected' holding the orphaned file inside the mmap until the end of the scope of 'expected' and the blob is written into a different file (at the path 'expected' used to be). We don't really need to hold on to the old file handle, so this just drops it.

subject: Skip single point contours with FreeType.
message:
I suppose the FreeType documentation doesn't explicitly state that it closes all contours (always provides the implicit closing segment), but it does do it and implies it does in the documentation about single points (which is oddly specific, I should write a better doc and propose it).

1. If a font has a <path> with (contours) like <(on,on), (on, ...)> then FreeType will report move, line, line, move. This will result in an SkPath with a moveTo, lineTo, close, and maybe a moveTo (depending on what follows). Dropping the final line is fine since any final line reported by FreeType is an implicit close (the SkPath close does the implicit line close already).

2. Sure, a 'line' reported by FreeType just before a 'move' must be an implicit close, so instead of an SkPath lineTo a more idiomatic SkPath close is emitted.

I'll have a test with a font with both of these cases in a bit to check this both here and on the other platforms before checking anything in.

subject: Make SkFontConfigInterface_direct and sysroot-aware
Make SkFontConfigInterface_direct and sysroot-aware
message:
This entire system seems quite bizarre, and I'm not sure why this is a thing in FontConfig that any user of FontConfig should ever be aware of. Are all users of FontConfig supposed to be updated to prepend this value to all filenames? That's quite a breaking change. Indeed, most of the point of a 'sysroot' is that apps don't need to know they're in one.

Looking at https://bugs.freedesktop.org/show_bug.cgi?id=59456 where this was introduced, the whole 'sysroot' thing is designed around running fc-cache with a sysroot parameter so that libfontconfig instances running inside an actual sysroot at that path would work. This code is 'undoing' that work (as far as I can tell), so why do it?

subject: SkUTF
message:
I suppose what I'm saying here is that either name them both SkUTF8_NextUnichar and go on a quest to remove the one argument version, or turn these into actual iterators or spans or ranges or whatever works nicely here. On the other hand, after looking around I can't say I see any shining examples of this sort of iterator that I like. I know we generally frown on overloading, but I'm fine with it since we're trying to get rid of one of them. On the other hand, maybe just SkUTF8_Next would be fine, since that is obviously (at least to me) going to read in a utf8 and return an SkUnichar. It's also shorter.

Note that icu has UTF8_NEXT which turns into http://icu-project.org/apiref/icu4c/utf8_8h.html#a27c3748113bc63347a7fa3a4b2c71029 . Note that this is more or less the same as the two argument version of SkUTF8_NextUnichar (except that its a macro so can do weird things).

subject: Fix SkFILEStream.
message: This new isAtEnd is quite aggressive. fOffset can never be greater than fSize (the size of the file when the SkFILEStream was created). Since that is checked first, isAtEnd will just always return false if we've tried to read or skip past the original end of the file. This second check is just a paranoid check in case someone shortened the underlying file out from under us. There's no point in checking the size of the file at any other time, it could just as easily race in other ways. It's theoretically possible that a debugger could notice that isAtEnd is being called, lengthen the file, then shorten the file afterword and end up causing something to loop, but that seems less likely.

subject: Add SkTypeface::getVariationDesignPosition.
message:
> I presume count and the return-type mean the same thing? (the number of axes). To match other skia apis, should they both be int?

As the comment states, the passed in 'count' is the number of entries in 'position' the caller has made available to write into. The return value is always the number of axes in the font, or -1 if there was an error. This allows the caller to avoid always calling twice by calling the first time with a small pre-allocated buffer. If it's big enough it will just be used the first time.

> I find the different names confusing. Why not getVariationCoordinates()?

I believe that for clarity 'Design' needs to be part of the name to distinguish from normalized coordinates. In the future we may wish to provide a means of obtaining the 'normalized' coordinates if they're available for less expensive inter-operation with HarfBuzz. The reason for 'Position' is that this is (quite pointedly) what the OpenType specification calls a specified location in the design variation space. I was actually just working on an actual type VariationPosition which would effectively be just a VariationCoordinate pointer and a count so that the names line up. It also makes the lines shorter and an number of other things somewhat simpler.

subject: GN: strip dead code everywhere, linker flag unification
message:
The gcc documentation says "you may have problems with debugging if you specify both this option and -g". Seems the result is that sometimes the debugger sometimes gets the instruction to line mapping wrong and sometimes loses local variables and vtable information, and this is sensitive to the order of the functions in a translation unit.

It seems that this sometimes causes extra loads because every global is now in a different section and the compiler doesn't know how they will end up laid out. So without data-sections a function which access globals will compute one offset to the global section (a load) and then read the globals as offsets from that (n + 1 loads). With data-sections every global requires a separate load to find its data section (and it's the only thing in it) and then a load to read it (2n loads). This probably doesn't make a lot of difference but something to keep in mind.

subject: GN: strip dead code everywhere, linker flag unification
message: These also being in debug seems a bit hostile to normal debugging by developers. There are a lot of 'getters' out there that will fold into identical code and the one that got picked will be the one the debugger shows when you step into any of them.

subject: Streamline skia.h construction.
message:
Is it enough to state here that this outputs depfile (aka "$skia_h.deps")? Then if the script is newer than the depfile at least the script is run to update the depfile. Of course, the 'skia.h' file is being written 'at the same time' so it doesn't seem like this would make a difference. However, this does create a build edge for creating the file and if it cannot be loaded it looks like it is considered out of date.

However, it turns out that this is discouraged. I don't entirely understand.

subject: Streamline skia.h construction.
message:
So the issue was that skia.h.d from previous versions started with 'skia.h:' instead of 'gen/skia.h:'. As a result, ninja gave the error "ninja: error: expected depfile 'gen/skia.h.d' to mention 'gen/skia.h', got 'skia.h'" and quit with exit code 1.

I seems quite awkward to recover from this. Would it be better if ninja ignored or warned on such an invalid depfile and then consider the target out of date? This would at least allow the target to re-run and try fixing up its depfile. Maybe this isn't possible because the depfile might be a non-generated edited outside the build thing? Or even generated by another build step, like https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja/issues/1090 .

Is there a reason why ninja can't just suck up the depfile and then delete it (similar to how it normally seems to with the compiler)? In other words, use ninja's 'deps = gcc' with 'depfile'. It seems gn surfaces this for toolchains, but not for actions...

Interestingly, if the depfile is edited externally or generated by the build anyway, the what ninja is doing is correct. You'll need to fix the file or the build and then that will regenerate the depfile and things should be good. However, if the build step itself is going to create the depfile, then it needs to be handled like the compiler depfile, where ninja sucks it in and deletes the file (and then errors and the target remains dirty if the depfile produced is invalid).

subject: Streamline skia.h construction.
message:
I think what I would like to be able to do is to be able to state the depfile 'gen/skia.h.d' depends on find_headers.py, then the build would notice that find_headers.py is newer than the depfile, so the depfile is out of date and needs to be updated (so any target which needs it is out of date) so don't even look at the depfile.

This is the same behavior that the compiler wants as well, all the compiler generated depfiles should be considered out of date if the compiler itself changes.

All that being said it turns out that ninja no longer treats this situation as an error, it is now a warning and an invalid depfile treats the target as out of date. It seems the ninja on the bot is more than a year old and isn't the one in the current depot_tools. Well have to see why that is independently, but it appears this isn't an actual issue in the present.
